lessons.title: Fill in the Blanks
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Vacuum Tubes were used in first generation computers
  • Charles Babbage is the Father of modern digital computer
  • Transistors replaced Vacuum Tubes in second generation
  • Analog computers process and represent continuous data
  • Supercomputer is the biggest and most powerful computer
  • Joystick is a pointing device with a vertical lever
  • RAM is also called a volatile memory

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.1 Fill in the Blanks

Q: Q.1 (i) The ______ technology was invented in the first generation of computers.

Ans: Vacuum Tubes

Q: Q.1 (ii) ______ is considered to be the “Father of modern digital computer”.

Ans: Charles Babbage

Q: Q.1 (iii) Transistors replaced ______ and were used in the second generation computers.

Ans: Vacuum Tubes

Q: Q.1 (iv) ______ computers are used to process and represent continuous data.

Ans: Analog

Q: Q.1 (v) ______ computer is the biggest in size and the most powerful computer.

Ans: Super

Q: Q.1 (vi) ______ is a pointing device with a vertical lever mounted on a base.

Ans: Joystick

Q: Q.1 (vii) The ______ is also called a volatile memory.

Ans: RAM

mcqs.q: Q.1 (i) The ______ technology was invented in the first generation of computers.
mcqs.why: Vacuum Tubes technology was used for memory and CPU circuitry in the first generation of computers from 1946 to 1959.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (ii) ______ is considered to be the “Father of modern digital computer”.
mcqs.why: Charles Babbage is considered the Father of modern digital computer, as stated in the solved fill in the blanks exercise.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (iii) Transistors replaced ______ and were used in the second generation computers.
mcqs.why: In the second generation, transistors replaced Vacuum Tubes and were smaller, faster, more reliable and used less power.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (iv) ______ computers are used to process and represent continuous data.
mcqs.why: Analog computers are used to process and represent continuous data, unlike digital computers which process discrete data.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (v) ______ computer is the biggest in size and the most powerful computer.
mcqs.why: The Super computer is the biggest in size and the most powerful computer, running one program at a time at very fast speed.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (vi) ______ is a pointing device with a vertical lever mounted on a base.
mcqs.why: A Joystick is a pointing input device with a vertical lever mounted on a base, mainly used for computer games and flight simulators.

mcqs.q: Q.1 (vii) The ______ is also called a volatile memory.
mcqs.why: RAM is called volatile memory because it retains information only when power is ON and all data is deleted when power is OFF.

mcqs.q: The ______ based on VLSI was used in fourth generation computers, with thousands of transistors on a single silicon chip.
mcqs.why: Fourth generation computers used the microprocessor based on VLSI, in which thousands of transistors were embedded on a single silicon chip.

mcqs.q: 1 Byte is represented in ______ bits.
mcqs.why: The solved answer states 1 Bit is a single binary digit and 1 Byte is represented in 8 bits, so the correct value is 8.

mcqs.q: The ______ contains the Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) used for booting the operating system.
mcqs.why: ROM is nonvolatile memory that contains the Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) used for booting the operating system.

lessons.title: Differentiate the Following
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Shareware is commercial trial software, Freeware is free of charge
  • Registers are inside the CPU, Cache stores frequently used data
  • Expansion slot is a socket on motherboard, card is the inserted board
  • RAM is volatile, ROM is nonvolatile and holds BIOS
  • System software controls hardware, Application software does user tasks
  • Register size can be 16, 32 or 64 bits

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Differentiate the Following

Q: Q.3 (i) Shareware vs. Freeware

Ans: Shareware is commercial and copyrighted software. It is usually offered either with certain features only available after the licence is purchased, or as a full version for a limited trial period, and once the trial period has passed the program may stop running until a licence is purchased. Freeware is computer software made available free of charge. A freeware application may or may not have its source code freely available, and it usually carries a licence that permits redistribution but has other restrictions, such as limitations on commercial use — for example, the program may be freely copied but never sold. Examples of freeware given in the book are Apache HTTP server, CCleaner, Skype and AOMEI Backupper.

Q: Q.3 (ii) Register vs. Cache memory

Ans: Registers are high-speed temporary storage locations inside the processor (CPU), used to hold data and instructions while they are being processed. The size of a register — 16, 32 or 64 bits — states how much information can be processed by the processor at once, and a register cannot handle information larger than its bit size. Cache memory is a memory that speeds up the process of computing by storing frequently used instructions and data, so the processor can get them quickly. There are generally two types of cache memory: L1 cache, which is built into the processor chip, and L2 cache, which is not a part of the processor chip.

Q: Q.3 (iii) Expansion slots vs. Expansion cards

Ans: An expansion slot is a socket on the motherboard where a circuit board, or expansion card, can be inserted to add new devices or capabilities to the computer. It provides an installation point for a hardware expansion card to be connected, and it allows the CPU to communicate with peripheral devices; common types are AGP (for video card), PCI (for network card, SCSI, sound card, video card) and ISA. An expansion card is a small circuit board that is inserted into an expansion slot on the motherboard to add new devices or capabilities to the computer. Expansion cards increase the functionality or capabilities of a system by adding more resources, and popular types include Radio Cards, Modem Cards, Network Interface Card, Sound Cards and Video Cards.

Q: Q.3 (iv) RAM vs. ROM

Ans: RAM (Random-Access Memory) is a volatile memory that can retain information only when the system power is ON; when the power is OFF, all the data is deleted. It is also called internal memory, primary memory or system memory, its data is accessed randomly instead of sequentially, and its access time is faster. ROM (Read-Only Memory) is a nonvolatile memory used in many electronic devices, and as its name indicates, the data stored in ROM can only be read. ROM contains the Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) used for booting the operating system and is commonly used as firmware; its types include Masked ROM (MROM), PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.

Q: Q.3 (v) System software vs. Application software

Ans: System software controls the working and the operations of the computer hardware and serves as the interface between the user, the application software and the hardware. It is fast in speed, has a complex design, interacts closely with the system and is implemented in a low-level language; its major categories are Operating System, Device Drivers, Utility programs and Language Processors. Application software is a set of programs, often called a software package, which work together to accomplish a task for the user, such as a spreadsheet package downloaded from the Web. Common types of application software are Productivity Software, Business Software, Entertainment Software and Educational Software.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • First generation used vacuum tubes, second used transistors
  • Third generation used ICs, fourth used microprocessor based on VLSI
  • Fifth generation uses ULSI, Artificial Intelligence and parallel processing
  • Mainframe handles thousands of users, Microcomputer is for a single user
  • Keyboard, Mouse, Joystick, Touch Screen and Scanner are input devices
  • CPU contains ALU, Control Unit and Registers
  • 1 Byte is 8 bits and 1 KiloByte is 1024 Bytes
  • Hard disk, Compact Disc, Memory Card and USB Flash Drive are storage devices

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Descriptive Questions

Q: Q.4 Give main features of each computer generation.

Ans: First Generation (1946–1959): vacuum tubes were used for memory and CPU circuitry; the computers were very large and costly, generated much heat, had slow I/O devices, needed AC, were non-portable and consumed much electricity; examples are ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC, IBM-701 and IBM-650. Second Generation (1959–1965): based on transistors, which were smaller, more compact, faster, reliable and consumed less power than vacuum tubes; the computers were reliable, smaller in size, faster than the first generation, costly and still required AC; examples are IBM 1620, IBM 7094, CDC 3600 and UNIVAC 1108. Third Generation (1965–1971): the Integrated Circuit (IC) replaced transistors, making computers smaller, faster, reliable and efficient; they were reliable, smaller, faster, expensive, required AC and consumed less electricity; examples are the IBM-360 series, Honeywell-6000 series, PDP and IBM-370/168. Fourth Generation (1971–1980): computers used the microprocessor based on VLSI, in which thousands of transistors were embedded on a single silicon chip; they were less expensive, portable, smaller in size, PCs were used, pipeline processing was introduced, no AC was required, the Internet was invented and networks developed, so computers became affordable; examples are STAR 1000, PDP 11 and CRAY-1 (Super Computer). Fifth Generation (1980–Present): the ULSI (Ultra Large Scale Integration) microprocessor replaced the VLSI microprocessor, with chips comprising ten million electronic components; its main features are the ULSI microprocessor, Artificial Intelligence (AI) development, Natural Language Processing (NLP) development, parallel processing advancement and affordability of computers; examples are Desktop, Laptop, NoteBook, Tablets and Smart Phone.

Q: Q.5 Explain different types of digital computers.

Ans: Digital computers process discrete data using discrete signals, convert data into machine codes with the help of translators, and usually use the binary number system, where '0' means 'Off' and '1' means 'On'. According to their size, speed, memory and peripheral support, they are classified as follows. (1) Mainframe Computers: a mainframe is a large-size, faster and expensive computer that can handle thousands of users simultaneously, executes many programs concurrently and supports many concurrent users; it is commonly used in big organizations, hospitals, airline companies, stock exchange companies and universities for processing a huge amount of data. (2) Minicomputers: also called mid-range computers, because they are smaller than mainframe and supercomputer but larger than microcomputer in size, speed, storage capacity, cost and other services; they support hundreds of users simultaneously and are mostly preferred by small-type business organizations, educational institutes and companies, though they have become obsolete nowadays. (3) Microcomputers: also called Personal Computers (PC), they are small in size, inexpensive and used by a single individual at a time; they are based on microprocessor technology on a single chip, which controls all the operations (input, processing, storage and output), and they are used for word processing, accounting, desktop publishing, spreadsheets and database management, while at home they are popular for playing games and surfing the Internet; their forms include Desktop Computers, Notebook Computers, Laptop and Palmtop. The book also notes the Supercomputer in this classification: unlike a mainframe, which executes parallel programs at a time, a supercomputer runs one program at a time but at a faster speed than a mainframe.

Q: Q.6 Write down the applications of computers in the following fields. i. Education ii. Business iii. Defence iv. Media

Ans: (i) Education: The computer plays a vital role in the education sector. It provides a software tool in the education system known as CBE (Computer Based Education), which includes control, delivery and analysis of the learning process in students. Online classes are possible by using computers in education, and university students spend an average of 4–5 hours a week web surfing for getting knowledge. (ii) Business: Because of its accuracy and efficiency of calculation, diligence and flexibility, the computer is an important part of all business organizations. It is used for placing orders of products, shipping information and price checks in retail stores, and also for pay slip calculations, budget estimation, sales analysis, financial database, online business training, managing the employee database, maintenance of stocks and records, the Internet as a common marketing tool, and online business meetings. (iii) Defence: Computers are very commonly used in the defence sector for communication, military planning and operation, digital weapons, controlling automated air-crafts, Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles (ICBMs) that use GPS (Global Positioning System) for targeting the missiles, designing and testing of new equipment, and simulations and trainings. (iv) Media: Computers are extensively used in print, electronic and mainstream media for typing and designing newspapers and magazines, video making and editing, animated movies, blogging, Usenet and video-conferencing.

Q: Q.7 Write note on any five input devices.

Ans: Input is any data or instructions entered into the memory of a computer with the help of input devices, and the data can be in any form such as text, graphics, audio or video. (1) Keyboard: a keyboard is used to enter data in the form of text and numbers into the computer; it has more than 100 buttons called keys, divided into sections such as Function keys, Special keys, Alphanumeric keys, Numeric keys and direction keys, a standard keyboard has a QWERTY layout, and a modern keyboard can be connected through a USB port. (2) Mouse: introduced by Douglas Engelbart in 1963 and known as the X-Y Position Indicator, the mouse is the most widely used pointing device on personal computers; it has two buttons and a scroll wheel, pressing the left button is called left click and pressing the right button is called right click, it may be wireless, and laptops have a built-in mouse called a touchpad. (3) Joystick: a joystick is a pointing input device with a vertical lever mounted on a base, and the lever usually includes buttons called triggers which activate certain events when pressed; joysticks are mainly used for computer games or controlling a machine or character in a flight simulator, and they connect to modern computers through a USB port. (4) Touch Screen: a touch screen is a touch-sensitive display input and output device that allows the user to interact with the computer using fingers or a stylus; it is an alternative to keyboard and mouse for navigation, takes input from the user and displays output at the same time, and is used in information kiosks in departmental stores, hotels, airports and museums, and on ATM machines for cash withdrawal and transfer of money. (5) Scanner: a scanner, or optical scanner, is a light-sensing input device that reads text or image from a surface and converts it into digital form; its quality is determined by its resolution and colour depth, many scanners include Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software which can convert an image of text into an editable text file, common types are Sheetfed scanner, handheld scanner and card scanner, and it connects to the computer via a USB port.

Q: Q.8 What is system unit? Explain main parts of system unit.

Ans: The system unit, also known as case, system box or main unit, is a case that contains all the main electronic components inside the computer, for example CPU, motherboard, hard drive and RAM. For a desktop computer, the electronic components and most storage devices such as hard disks and CD-ROM drives reside inside the system unit, while for a laptop computer the system unit houses almost all of its components including the keyboard, pointing device and monitor. Its main part is the motherboard: the motherboard or system-board, first released in 1981 and used in the IBM Personal Computer, is the main circuit board in the system unit and the main circuitry of the system. Several different types of chips, such as CPU and memory chips, are found on the motherboard, and it also contains expansion slots into which other circuit boards can be inserted for the expansion of the computer system, so it allows communication between CPU, RAM and other hardware components. The components of the motherboard are expansion slots (PCI Express, PCI and AGP), CPU socket, memory slot, Serial ATA connections and coin cell battery (CMOS backup battery).

Q: Q.9 What is CPU? Explain the main parts of CPU.

Ans: The processor, or Central Processing Unit (CPU) or microprocessor, is the electronic device that interprets and carries out the instructions that tell the computer how to work, and it performs all the tasks that are received from the hardware or software. The CPU is usually contained on a single chip and is often called a microprocessor, and a microprocessor usually contains the Control Unit (CU), the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU) and registers. (a) Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU): the ALU performs arithmetic, comparison and logical operations — arithmetic operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, while comparison operations involve comparing one data item to another to determine if the first item is greater than, equal to, or less than the other item; the processed information of the ALU is sent to the computer memory. (b) Control Unit (CU): the CU is a circuitry that directs and coordinates most of the operations in the processor; it guides the logic unit, memory and I/O devices how to respond to instructions received from a program, and for every instruction the control unit repeats a set of basic operations called the machine cycle or instruction cycle. (c) Registers: registers are high-speed temporary storage locations used to hold data and instructions; the size of a register, which can be 16, 32 or 64 bits, states how much information can be processed by a processor at once.

Q: Q.10 How many storage devices are used? Briefly discuss any three storage devices.

Ans: Storage devices refer to the media on which data, instructions and information are stored; storage is also known as backing storage or secondary storage, and it is necessary because memory is volatile and usually limited. The book lists four common storage devices: Hard disk, Compact disk, Memory card and USB Flash drive. (1) Hard Disk Drive (HDD): a hard disk is a large backing storage device consisting of several inflexible, circular disks called platters, on which items are stored electronically; in most desktop and laptop computers it is housed inside the system unit and is considered a fixed disk because it is not portable, and hard disks are sealed tightly to keep out contaminants such as dust and smoke particles, which may result in a head crash. (2) Compact Disc (CD): a Compact Disc is a flat, round, portable storage medium that is usually 4.75 inches in diameter and less than one-twentieth of an inch thick, and compact discs store items by using a laser beam. (3) Memory Card: a memory card, also known as a Secure Digital (SD) card, is a small-sized electronic memory backing storage medium; data can be read or written on an SD card using a specialized card reader, they are commonly used in many electronic devices including digital cameras, mobile phones, laptop computers, MP3 players and video game consoles, and they can retain data without power. The fourth device, the USB Flash Drive, is a flash memory data storage device integrated with a USB interface; it is removable and rewritable and physically much smaller than other storage media.

Q: Q.11 What is computer memory? Explain different types of computer memory in detail.

Ans: Memory is a temporary area for holding data, instructions and information; it is also known as main memory or primary memory. A computer usually loads the data and instructions from storage into memory and then executes them, memory has a much faster access time than backing storage, memory can be volatile or nonvolatile, and its size is measured by the number of bytes available for use. The basic measurement unit of memory is the byte: 1 Bit (Binary Digit) is a single binary digit that can be either 0 or 1, 1 Byte is represented in 8 bits, and the higher units are 1 KiloByte (KB) = 1024 Bytes, 1 MegaByte (MB) = 1024 KiloByte, 1 GigaByte (GB) = 1024 MegaByte, 1 TeraByte (TB) = 1024 GigaByte and 1 PetaByte (PB) = 1024 TeraByte. (1) RAM (Random-Access Memory): RAM is a volatile memory that can retain information only when the system power is ON, and when the power is OFF all the data is deleted; it is also called internal memory, primary memory or system memory, the data in RAM is accessed randomly instead of sequentially, its access time is faster, and RAM chips are usually packaged on a small circuit board inserted into the motherboard. (2) ROM (Read-Only Memory): ROM is a nonvolatile memory used in many electronic devices, and the data stored in ROM can only be read; ROM contains the Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) used for booting the operating system, ROM is commonly used as firmware, and its types are Masked ROM (MROM), Programmable Read Only Memory (PROM), Erasable and Programmable Read Only Memory (EPROM) and Electrically Erasable and Programmable Read Only Memory (EEPROM). (3) Cache Memory: most computers today use cache memory, which speeds up the process of computing by storing frequently used instructions and data; there are generally two types of cache memory — L1 cache is built into the processor chip, while L2 cache is not a part of the processor chip.

Q: Q.12 Draw the block diagram of a computer.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The block diagram (Figure 1.56, Basic Operations of a Computer) shows four units joined by two kinds of flow — a solid arrow for Data flow and a dotted line for Control flow. On the left, Data enters the Input Unit. The Input Unit sends the data by a data-flow arrow into the Storage Unit, drawn as one block at the top centre divided into two parts: Primary Storage below and Secondary Storage above, with a two-way data-flow arrow between them, so data and results move between primary and secondary storage. From the Storage Unit, a data-flow arrow goes to the right into the Output Unit, and the Output Unit gives out Information. Below the Storage Unit is the Central Processing block, divided into the Control Unit (CU) on top and the Arithmetic and Logical Unit (ALU) below it. The Control Unit is joined by dotted control-flow lines to the Input Unit, to the Storage Unit and to the Output Unit, showing that the CU controls and coordinates all of them, while the ALU carries out the processing. In this way the computer performs its four basic operations: Input (accepting data from the user through input devices), Processing (manipulation of data into useful form, performed by the processor), Storage (storing or retaining data, information or instructions so the user can retain and retrieve it whenever required) and Output (the result of the transformation process, which displays information to the user either in soft form or in hard form).

Q: Q.13 Write down three real life examples of application software used in different organizations.

Ans: Application software is a set of programs, often called a software package, which work together to accomplish a task for the user. Three real-life examples from the book are: (1) Productivity software in offices and homes — word processing software such as MS-Word, WordPad and Notepad is used for creating and editing documents, spreadsheet software such as Excel and Apple Numbers is used for calculations, and presentation software such as Microsoft PowerPoint and Open Office Presentation is used for making presentations; database software examples are Oracle and MS Access. (2) Business software in business organizations — business packages are used to perform a variety of business tasks, and common types include book-keeping programs, accounting packages, personal finance software and payroll record software. (3) Educational software in schools and other educational organizations — educational software aims to teach and educate users and helps to deliver education material and track progress; its common types are Learning Management System (LMS), Campus Management System (CMS), classroom management software, Desktop Publishing and referencing software. The book's software categories figure also gives specific-purpose application examples used in organizations: a Reservation system, an Attendance System, a Billing System and a Report Card Generator.

Q: Q.14 Briefly discuss the responsibilities of system analyst?

Ans: A system analyst is a person who is responsible for the development and research of a business, department or project, and recommends software and systems. He finds the problems, explores solutions and coordinates the developer and customer to meet business or other requirements. Analysts are familiar with hardware, operating systems, programming and software. A system analyst can also configure and plan the computer systems and infrastructure for an organization, including performing testing.

lessons.title: Differentiate the Following
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Single-user has one user at a time, Multi-user has many users via server
  • UNIX from 1960s Bell Labs, Linux is its updated free open-source form
  • Batch jobs are queued in batches, Time sharing gives each user a time slice
  • Files store data, folders store files and other folders
  • Copy leaves original in place, Cut removes original after paste
  • CLI needs typed memorized commands, GUI uses menus buttons icons with mouse

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Differentiate the following

Q: Q.3 (i) Single-user vs. Multi-user Operating System.

Ans: Single-user Operating System: It has only one user at any given time, e.g. a computer at home. In its single-tasking form (Palm OS, MS-DOS) it performs only one task at a time and needs less memory space, while in its single-user/multitasking form (Windows OS, Macintosh OS) one user does many tasks simultaneously. Multi-user Operating System: Many users access the same Operating System at the same time from different machines through a single network server, called the Terminal server. It is used in businesses and offices where different users need the same resources, it is fast and time-saving, but if a client loses its connection to the server it cannot perform any task. Examples are UNIX, Linux, Windows and Ubuntu.

Q: Q.3 (ii) Unix vs. Linux Operating System.

Ans: UNIX: It was first developed in the 1960s by the MULTICS team at Bell Laboratories. It is a command driven, multi-user and multi-tasking Operating System for servers and desktops, and it has been in use for more than three decades. Linux: It is an updated form of the UNIX Operating System and is a GUI Operating System. It is as user friendly as Windows, it is a free and open-source Operating System whose source code is freely available to download, edit and distribute, and it is now commonly used in offices and homes.

Q: Q.3 (iii) Batch processing vs. Time sharing processing system

Ans: Batch processing system: The Operating System works through a series of programs/tasks in a queue. The user prepares his job on punch cards and submits it to the computer operator, who collects jobs from different users, sorts them into batches with similar needs and submits the batches to the processor one by one, so all jobs of one batch are executed together without manual intervention, e.g. processing of monthly utility bills. Time sharing processing system: A number of users at different terminals simultaneously use a single powerful computer for different purposes. The CPU allocates an individual slice of time to each user in turn, so every user gets the impression that he is the sole user of the system, although the response time for each terminal declines as the number of users increases.

Q: Q.3 (iv) File vs. folder.

Ans: File: A file is a collection of related information, or a resource for storing information, and it can be stored permanently on a backing storage device like a hard disk. Every file has a name for its identity, made of the file name and the extension after the '.' which tells the computer in which application the file can be opened, e.g. .doc or .docx opens in Microsoft Word. Folder: A folder is a named collection of related files that can be retrieved, moved and manipulated as one entity, and it is used to store and manage files or sub-folders. The basic difference given in the book is that files store data, while folders store files and other folders.

Q: Q.3 (v) Copy vs. Cut command.

Ans: Copy command: To copy a file/folder, select it, right-click on it and select the Copy command from the menu; then go to the destination folder/location, right-click and select Paste, and the file/folder is pasted there while the original also remains at its first place, so the item exists at both places. Cut command: To move a file/folder, select it, right-click on it and select the Cut command from the menu; then go to the destination folder/location, right-click and select Paste, and the file/folder is pasted there. With Cut the item is removed from its original location, so it exists only at the new place.

Q: Q.3 (vi) CLI vs. GUI Operating System

Ans: CLI (Command Line Interface): The user types in commands to make the computer do something, so the user must memorize the commands and type them correctly. It uses only a keyboard to navigate, does not use a mouse, is quicker than GUI but difficult to operate; DOS and UNIX are its examples. GUI (Graphical User Interface): Every object is represented by a small graphic, picture or symbol, and the user selects commands from various menus, buttons and icons using a mouse. It is a user-friendly interface because the graphical representation of commands is much easier to understand and use; Windows, Macintosh and Linux are its examples.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Operating System manages memory, I/O, files, resources and users
  • DOS is non-graphical command line OS for IBM compatible computers

  • Macintosh in 1984 was first widely-sold PC with a GUI

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.4 What is an Operating System? Explain some common tasks or functions of an Operating System.

Q: Q.4 What is an Operating System? Explain some common tasks or functions of an Operating System.

Ans: An Operating System is the system software that runs all the application programs and utilities and provides an interface between the application programs and the computer hardware. It is a set of programs containing instructions that coordinate all the activities of the computer, it manages all the other programs and the resources attached with the system such as memory, processor and input/output devices, and without it a computer is useless. Its common functions are: (a) Memory Management — it manages main memory, keeps track of which part is in use and by whom, allocates memory when a program requests it and clears programs from memory when they are no longer required. (b) I/O Management — it performs device management through drivers and input/output controllers, tracks the connected devices and decides which program may access which device and in what order. (c) File Management — it lets the user locate and manipulate data files on the hard disk, keeps track of the locations of all files, and helps in moving, renaming, editing and deleting files, organizing them into directories and sub-directories like a tree. (d) Resource Management — it manages resources like CPU time, memory, files and I/O devices, allocates and de-allocates them to a process and performs process scheduling. (e) Users Management — it provides security to user data, prevents unauthorized access through passwords and checks the persons who log into the system.

Exercise — Q.5 Write short note on the following.

Q: Q.5 (i) DOS

Ans: DOS (Disk Operating System) was the first widely-installed Operating System for personal computers. It is a non-graphical, command line Operating System created for IBM compatible computers, in which the user types commands such as C:\> DIR, C:\> CLS and C:\> COPY at the DOS prompt and must memorize them. Although DOS is not commonly used today, the command shell is still used through Microsoft Windows to support existing DOS applications, and in Windows the Command Prompt is opened from Start Menu > Windows System > Command Prompt.

Q: Q.5 (ii) UNIX

Ans: UNIX is an Operating System which was first developed in the 1960s by the MULTICS team at the Bell laboratories. It is a command driven, multi-user and multi-tasking system used for servers and desktops. UNIX has been in use for more than three decades, and Linux is its updated form.

Q: Q.5 (iii) Macintosh

Ans: The Macintosh, often called "the Mac", was introduced in 1984 by Apple Computer and was the first widely-sold personal computer with a GUI. It has a user-friendly computer interface in which the user uses the mouse as an input device to access any file or folder by double clicking on it. The Mac Operating System provides similar functions and services like Linux and Windows, but it is supported on Apple based PCs and is not operated on x86 architecture.

Q: Q.5 (iv) Windows

Ans: Windows is a GUI Operating System developed by Microsoft, which contains graphics and icons and is commonly navigated by using a computer mouse. It can be used to store files, run software, play games, watch videos and connect to the Internet, and it was released for both home and professional computing. Microsoft introduced its first version as 1.0, and Microsoft Windows was first introduced in November 1985; Windows 10 is the version whose desktop and installation are described in this unit.

Exercise — Q.6 Explain different components/features of Graphical User Interface (GUI).

Q: Q.6 Explain different components/features of Graphical User Interface (GUI).

Ans: In a GUI, each and every object is represented by a small size graphic, picture or symbol, and the user selects commands from various menus, buttons and icons using a mouse, which makes it a user-friendly interface. Its main components/features described in this unit are: (1) Icons — an icon is an informative picture, a small graphic or symbol used to perform an action; by double-clicking an application icon the program opens, and icons represent software packages, documents and hardware devices. The basic Windows icons are This PC (shows all resources of the computer including drives, control panel and data), Recycle Bin (keeps files deleted accidentally or intentionally, which can be restored before permanent deletion), Control Panel (the control center for viewing and changing settings, adding or removing software and hardware, and setting up network connections and user accounts), Network (used to view and set the network resources of the computer) and User Account (used to log in to Windows, with a separate account possible for each person sharing the computer). (2) Menus — lists of options/commands on the screen from which the user selects a choice, and which lead to other screens. (3) Buttons — clickable controls in windows and dialog boxes (such as OK, Cancel, Next and Install now in the setup screens) used to confirm or perform an action. (4) Mouse/pointer — the pointing device used to select icons, menus and buttons instead of typing commands. (5) Desktop and Windows — the graphical working screen (e.g. the Windows 10, Mac OS and Linux desktops shown in the unit) on which icons are displayed and programs open in windows, with the Start Menu and taskbar used to start programs and search.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A spreadsheet organises, formats and calculates data in rows and columns.
  • MS Word, WordPerfect, Open Office Word and Google Docs are word processors.
  • Symbols are inserted from Insert tab, Symbols group, More Symbols.
  • Equations are written with Insert New Equation on the Insert tab.
  • Headers sit in the top margin and footers in the bottom margin.
  • The ruler is shown from the View tab in Print Layout view.
  • A hyperlink links to another part of the document or to a web page.
  • A function begins with =, then the function name, then arguments in parentheses.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Give short answers to the following questions.

Q: Q.3 (i) Define a Spreadsheet software.

Ans: A spreadsheet is a computer application (Microsoft Office Excel 2016 is the commonly used spreadsheet software) that displays data in multiple cells, usually in a two-dimensional matrix or grid consisting of rows and columns. It is used to organize, format and calculate data. Each cell contains alphanumeric text, numeric values or formulae, and the sheet automatically re-calculates after a change to a single cell, which is why spreadsheets are frequently used for financial information.

Q: Q.3 (ii) Give few examples of Word processing software.

Ans: The book names MS Word, Word Perfect, Open Office Word and Google Docs as examples of word processor software. Its Word Processor Software list also includes Abiword, Apple iWork, Apple TextEdit, Corel WordPerfect, Dropbox Paper, LibreOffice, Microsoft WordPad, SoftMaker FreeOffice, OpenOffice and Kingsoft WPS Office. Microsoft Word is the most widely used word processing software.

Q: Q.3 (iii) How you can insert a symbol in a Word document?

Ans: In Word 2016 mathematical symbols can be inserted into equations or simply at a blank location. Steps: (1) On the Insert tab, in the Symbols group, click the arrow next to Symbol and then click More Symbols. (2) The Symbol dialog box appears. (3) Click the arrow next to the Subset name and click the name of the symbol set you want to display. (4) Select the required symbol and click the Insert button to insert it in the document.

Q: Q.3 (iv) How Equation Editor can be used in Word document?

Ans: Word 2016 includes built-in support for writing and changing equations through the Equation Editor. To write a new equation: on the Insert tab, in the Symbols group, click the arrow next to Equations and then click Insert New Equation, and type the equation. To insert a frequently used or preformatted equation: on the Insert tab, in the Symbols group, click the arrow next to Equations and then click the required equation from the built-in menu.

Q: Q.3 (v) How you can insert header, footer and ruler in Word window?

Ans: Header and Footer: (1) Select the Insert tab. (2) Click either the Header or Footer command; a menu of built-in options appears. (3) Click Blank (or another built-in style), place the cursor in the header (top margin) or footer (bottom margin) and type the desired text such as page number, date or document name; the Design tab with Header and Footer tools becomes active. For page numbers, on the Insert tab select the Page Number command from the Header & Footer group and specify the position. Ruler: the ruler is shown from the View tab — in Print Layout view select Ruler in the Show group; the horizontal ruler appears under the Ribbon and the vertical ruler at the left, and they are used to align text vertically/horizontally and to adjust table column widths and row heights.

Q: Q.3 (vi) What is the use of hyperlink in a Word document?

Ans: A hyperlink is a piece of text or an image in a document that can connect readers to another portion of the document or to a web page. Links are useful for directing others who read the document to a specific site, or for adding a bibliography to a school assignment. Sometimes a link to a location in the same document is needed, which is done with the Place in This Document option. The shortcut Ctrl+K also inserts a hyperlink on highlighted text.

Q: Q.3 (vii) What is a function in Excel? Explain different parts of function with one example.

Ans: A function is a predefined formula that performs calculations using specific values in a particular order, and it saves time because the user does not have to write the whole formula. Parts of a function: (1) Equal sign — all functions begin with the = sign. (2) Function name — written after the = sign, e.g. SUM. (3) Argument — the cell range or cell references enclosed in parentheses; if there is more than one argument, each is separated by a comma. Example with one argument: =SUM(A3:A9) adds the range of cells A3 through A9; example with more than one argument: =SUM(A3:A9, B3:B5). Common functions are SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX and MIN.

Q: Q.3 (viii) What is the purpose of using Urdu editor?

Ans: Urdu editor is application software used to create documents in Urdu, the national language of Pakistan. It is very useful for developing documents like Urdu newspapers, magazines, pamphlets and leaflets, and offers features like fonts, font styles, font sizes and page layouts. Examples are Katib, InPage and Urdu Editor; InPage is the most commonly used and popular Urdu editor, and MS Word 2016 also allows typing Urdu text.

Q: Q.3 (ix) What is purpose of office automation software?

Ans: Office automation software is used to do office work on the computer quickly and in a professional way. Word processing is used for writing, editing, formatting and printing reports and documents such as memos, letters, notes, books, newspapers and magazines, and documents can be saved, displayed, printed and forwarded through email. Spreadsheet software is used to organize, format and calculate data, especially financial information, and to represent data graphically through charts. Urdu editors are used to create Urdu documents such as newspapers and magazines.

lessons.title: Differentiate the Following
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • WordArt decorates text while Clip Art inserts a ready-made image.
  • Save keeps the same name and location; Save As gives a new name or location.
  • Paste inserts everything; Paste Special pastes only chosen attributes.
  • A formula is user-written; a function is a predefined formula.
  • A page break starts a new page; a section break changes formatting.
  • A workbook holds worksheets; a worksheet is one sheet of cells.
  • Copy leaves the original in place; Cut removes it from the source.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.4 Differentiate the following:

Q: Q.4 (i) Word Art vs. Clipart

Ans: WordArt is a more stylish type of text: it is a gallery of text styles that lets you change the style and border of the text to make it attractive and fancy, with styles such as embossed, bordered and shadowed text, and it can be moved almost anywhere and resized (Insert tab > Text group > WordArt). Clip Art, on the other hand, is art or an image created by numerous artists to fit different categories such as people, animals, school, fruits and vegetables, which is inserted into a document as a ready-made picture (Insert tab > Illustrations group > Online Pictures). In short, WordArt decorates text, while Clipart inserts a ready-made image.

Q: Q.4 (ii) Save vs. Save As

Ans: Save is used when the document is to keep the same name and the same storage location; it simply stores the latest changes in the existing file (File tab > Save, or Ctrl+S, or the Save icon on the Quick Access Toolbar). Save As is used when changes have been made and the user wants to give the file a new filename or a new storage location; Save As must be selected to give the document the new name and location, keeping the original file separate.

Q: Q.4 (iii) Paste vs. Paste Special

Ans: Paste inserts the whole copied or cut contents, with all their formatting, at the new location (Home tab > Clipboard group > Paste, or Ctrl+V); whatever was placed on the clipboard is pasted completely. Paste Special (in Excel) is used to copy complex items and paste them into the same or another worksheet using only specific attributes of the copied data, or a mathematical operation to be applied to it. Through its dialog box the user can choose to paste only All, Formulas, Values, Formats, Comments or Validation, and can also apply operations such as Add, Subtract, Multiply or Divide.

Q: Q.4 (iv) Formula vs. Function

Ans: A formula is an equation (an expression entered in a cell) that performs a calculation using values in the worksheet, e.g. =60+70 or =B2+B3 typed by the user beginning with an equal sign. A function is a predefined (ready-made) formula that performs calculations using specific values in a particular order, e.g. =SUM(A3:A9). Functions save time because the user does not have to write the formula; common functions are SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX and MIN.

Q: Q.4 (v) Page break vs. Section break

Ans: A Page break moves text to a new page before reaching the end of a page, i.e. the following text simply starts on the next page. A Section break creates a barrier between parts of the document for formatting purposes, so that different parts of the same document can have different formatting. Both are inserted by placing the cursor where the break is to appear, selecting the Layout tab, clicking the Breaks command and choosing the required break option.

Q: Q.4 (vi) Workbook vs. Worksheet

Ans: A Workbook is the Excel file that stores data and may contain numerous worksheets; it is the combination of worksheets and by default it has one worksheet. A Worksheet is a single sheet inside the workbook, made of rows and columns of cells in which data is actually entered; its name appears on the Sheet tab at the bottom-left of the window, and clicking a Sheet tab activates that worksheet for editing.

Q: Q.4 (vii) Cut vs. Copy

Ans: Copy (Copy-Paste) is used to take a duplicate of the text by copying it and pasting it where required; it does not remove the text from the source location, so the text remains at both places (select text, Home tab > Copy or Ctrl+C, then Paste or Ctrl+V). Cut (Cut-Paste or Move) is used to move text from one place (source) to another place (destination) and removes the text from the source location (select text, Home tab > Cut or Ctrl+X, then Paste). In both cases the cut or copied text is first placed on the clipboard, the temporary storage place in computer memory.

lessons.title: Definitions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A spreadsheet displays data in a two-dimensional grid of rows and columns.
  • A workbook is the combination of worksheets and has one worksheet by default.
  • A worksheet is a single sheet where data is entered in rows and columns.
  • A cell is the intersection of a row and a column.
  • A cell address combines the column letter and row number, such as D4.
  • A relative reference adjusts on pasting; an absolute reference uses the $ sign.
  • Every formula begins with the equal sign.
  • Common functions are SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX and MIN.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.7 Define the following.

Q: Q.7 (i) Define Spreadsheet.

Ans: A spreadsheet is a computer application that displays data in multiple cells, usually in a two-dimensional matrix or grid consisting of rows and columns. It is used to organize, format and calculate data; each cell contains alphanumeric text, numeric values or formulae, and the entire sheet re-calculates automatically after a change to a single cell. Microsoft Office Excel 2016 is the commonly used spreadsheet software.

Q: Q.7 (ii) Define Workbook.

Ans: A workbook is the Excel file that stores data and may contain numerous worksheets. Key Points define it as the combination of worksheets, and by default a workbook has one worksheet. Each new workbook shows one worksheet tab, and worksheets inside it can be added, selected through their Sheet tabs and renamed.

Q: Q.7 (iii) Define Worksheet.

Ans: A worksheet is a single sheet of a workbook in which data is entered in rows and columns of cells. Its name appears on the Sheet tab at the bottom-left of the spreadsheet; by default the name on the tab is Sheet1, and when the user clicks on the respective Sheet tab, that worksheet is activated for editing.

Q: Q.7 (iv) Define Cell.

Ans: The cell is the basic unit of a worksheet for entering data. A cell is the intersection of a row and a column; each rectangle in the worksheet is called a cell. The user clicks a cell to select it and enters data (text, numeric or formula) into it with the keyboard, and the data appears in the cell and in the formula bar.

Q: Q.7 (v) Define Cell address.

Ans: A cell address is the location (name) of a specific cell on a worksheet, based on the column and row it is in, and it can be found in the Name Box. Columns are identified by capital alphabets and numbers indicate the rows; for example, the cell at the intersection of column D and row 4 is D4.

Q: Q.7 (vi) Define Cell reference.

Ans: A cell reference is the cell address used as part of a formula: instead of entering specific numbers into a formula, the cell address refers to a specific cell, e.g. the formula in cell D7 using =D2:D6 style references. References are of two types: a relative reference automatically adjusts to the new location when the formula is pasted into different cells, while an absolute reference always refers to the same cell or range and is designated by a dollar sign ($) before the column and/or row, e.g. $A$2.

Q: Q.7 (vii) Define Formula.

Ans: A formula is an equation (expression) entered in a cell that performs a calculation using values in the worksheet, such as numeric calculation, logical comparison or text string manipulation. Every formula begins with the equal sign (=), e.g. =60+70 adds two numbers, and =B2+B3 adds the contents of two cells; subtraction, multiplication and division operators can also be used.

Q: Q.7 (viii) Define Function.

Ans: A function is a predefined formula that performs calculations using specific values in a particular order, and it begins with the = sign, followed by the function name and its argument in parentheses, e.g. =SUM(A3:A9). Functions save time because the formula does not have to be written out. Commonly used statistical functions are SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX and MIN.

Q: Q.7 (ix) Define Chart.

Ans: A chart is a tool used in Excel to represent data graphically; Key Points define charts as the graphical presentation of data from a worksheet. Charts let the audience more easily understand the meaning behind the numbers in the spreadsheet and show comparisons and trends among the data. Two types of charts are created in Excel: the embedded chart and the chart sheet.

lessons.title: Word and Excel Window
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Excel window parts include Name Box, Formula Bar, Sheet Tab and Zoom Slider.
  • The Word Title bar shows the document name at the centre.
  • The Word Ribbon contains nine tabs with related command groups.
  • The Quick Access Toolbar holds Save, Undo and Redo commands.
  • The Zoom Slider zooms the document view from 10% to 500%.
  • The Status Bar shows the current page and word count.
  • Autofill fills cells following a pattern using the fill handle.
  • Dragging the fill handle turns the white cross into a thin black cross.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.5 Label different parts of the following Excel window.

Q: Q.5 Label different parts of the following Excel window.

Ans: The labelled parts of the Excel window (Figure 3.67) are: Top row, left to right — Quick Access Toolbar, Ribbon, Title bar, Minimize Button, Maximize Button, Close Button. Left side, top to bottom — Name Box, Active Cell, Formula Bar. Bottom row, left to right — Column, Row, Sheet Tab, Status Bar, Horizontal Scroll Bar, Zoom Slider, Vertical Scroll Bar. The Ribbon is used to navigate through Excel and access the various Excel commands, the worksheet tabs are at the bottom-left, and the Page View, Zoom slider and Horizontal scroll bar are at the bottom-right of the spreadsheet.

Exercise — Q.6 Explain different components of Word window.

Q: Q.6 Explain different components of Word window.

Ans: (i) Title bar: the topmost bar; it displays the Quick Access Toolbar at its left, the name of the current document at the center and Control Buttons at its right side. (ii) Ribbon: the second bar below the Title bar, containing nine Tabs (File, Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Mailings, Review, View); each tab displays related command Groups, e.g. Home tab has Clipboard, Font, Paragraph, Styles and Editing groups. (iii) Control Buttons: at the top-right of the Title bar, used to minimize, maximize or close the Word document. (iv) Quick Access Toolbar: at the top-left of the Title bar, containing quick-access commands like Save, Undo and Redo, and more commands can be added by customizing it. (v) Ruler: used to align text vertically/horizontally in the document. (vi) Document window: the main area used to create the document, where text and images are entered; the blinking vertical line is the cursor, which defines the insertion point. (vii) Vertical and Horizontal Scroll Bars: used to move around the document vertically and horizontally. (viii) Zoom Slider: used to zoom in or zoom out the view of the document, from 10% to 500%. (ix) Status Bar: located at the bottom of the Word window; it gives information about the present status of the document, such as the current page and the number of words in the document.

Exercise — Q.8 What is the purpose of Autofill command in Excel?

Q: Q.8 What is the purpose of Autofill command in Excel?

Ans: The Autofill command in Excel is applied for the automatic filling of data: it fills cells that follow a specified pattern, or it fills cells based on data in other cells, without typing each entry. To use it, position the cursor over the fill handle until the large white cross becomes a thin black cross, drag it until all the cells to be filled are highlighted, and release the mouse button — all the selected cells are filled automatically with the information from the original cell. When a formula is entered into a cell and Enter is pressed, the formula can also copy automatically to the rows in the table in this way.

lessons.title: Lab Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Lab Activities

Q: Lab Activity 1 (i): Create a new document on the topic "Myself" and Save it.

Ans: Start Word (Start > search 'W' > Word 2016, or type 'word' in the search bar and press Enter). A new blank document is created by default; or click New in the File menu, then click Blank Document (or press Ctrl+N). Type the text on 'Myself', then save it: File tab > Save or Save As, or press Ctrl+S, or click the Save icon on the Quick Access Toolbar, give a file name and location.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (ii): Copy and paste a paragraph within a document.

Ans: Select the paragraph (click the left mouse button and drag over the text, then release; or use Shift + Right Arrow, or Ctrl+A for the whole document). Choose Copy on the Home tab in the Clipboard group, or press Ctrl+C — the text is copied onto the clipboard and stays at the source. Move the cursor to the new place and click, then choose Paste on the Home tab in the Clipboard group, or press Ctrl+V; the paragraph appears at the new location.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (iii): Cut and paste a line within a document.

Ans: Select the line to cut. Choose Cut on the Home tab in the Clipboard group, or press Ctrl+X — the line is cut onto the clipboard and removed from the source. Move the mouse cursor to the place where the text is to be placed and click, then choose Paste on the Home tab in the Clipboard group, or press Ctrl+V; the line appears at the new location (this is the Cut-Paste / Move option).

Q: Lab Activity 1 (iv): Open a saved document and print it.

Ans: Open: click the File menu and click Open, or press Ctrl+O, and select the saved document. Print: make sure the printer is on and ready; click the Print command in the File tab, or press Ctrl+P; the Print window opens; click Print and the document will be printed.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (v): Delete the folder "My Personal files" from the desktop.

Ans: Deleting means removing the item, as text is removed from a document with the Delete/Backspace keys. On the desktop, select (click) the folder 'My Personal files' and press the Delete key on the keyboard; the folder is removed from the desktop. (The unit teaches deletion through the Delete key: select the item to be deleted, then press Delete.)

Q: Lab Activity 1 (vi): Insert and position pictures within a document.

Ans: Click in the document where you want to insert the picture. On the Insert tab, in the Illustrations group, click Pictures; the Insert Picture dialog box appears; locate and double-click the picture to insert it. The picture can then be positioned in the document as required. Pictures and Clip Art can also be inserted from a Clip Art website or copied from a web page.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (vii): Insert word Art in your document.

Ans: Open Microsoft Word. In the Ribbon, click the Insert tab. In the Text group, click the WordArt option. Select the type of WordArt you want to add to the document (e.g. embossed, bordered or shadowed style), type the text; the WordArt can be moved almost anywhere and its size adjusted. To delete it later, select the WordArt and press the Delete key.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (viii): Using Table feature, create your class time table.

Ans: Place the mouse cursor where you want to add the table. Click the Insert tab in the Ribbon. Click the Table button and select how many cells, rows and columns the time table needs, or click Insert Table and enter the number of columns and rows. Type the days, periods and subjects in the cells; rows/columns can be added (right-click > Insert > Insert Rows Above/Below, Insert Columns to the Left/Right), deleted, resized, and borders and shading applied to format the time table.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (ix): Change the page size and margins in your document.

Ans: Page size/orientation: click the Layout tab on the Ribbon; in the Page Setup group click the Orientation, Size or Columns drop-down menu and click the appropriate choice. Margins: in the Ribbon click the Layout tab and then click the Margins option; select one of the preset margin options or click Custom Margins to specify the Top, Bottom, Left and Right margins you want, then click OK to set the selected margins.

Q: Lab Activity 1 (x): Insert hyperlink in your document.

Ans: Open Microsoft Word and type the appropriate text. Select (with mouse or keyboard) the text you want to turn into a hyperlink. In the Ribbon click the Insert tab; in the Links group click the Hyperlink option. In the Insert Hyperlink window, type the web page address in the Address text box and click OK; the selected text or image now becomes a hyperlink. (Shortcut: Ctrl+K.)

Q: Lab Activity 2 (i): Create a New blank workbook with four sheets and name it "My workbook".

Ans: Start Excel (Click Start, search for alphabet 'E', click Excel 2016); a new blank workbook opens with one worksheet by default. Add sheets with the + (New Sheet) button next to the Sheet tabs until there are four sheets (Sheet1–Sheet4). Save the file with the name 'My workbook' (File > Save/Save As or Ctrl+S). Worksheets can be renamed by right-clicking the Sheet tab, choosing Rename and typing a new name.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (ii): Add some data in the sheet1 and save it.

Ans: Click Sheet1 tab to activate it. Click a cell to select it (its address appears in the Name Box) and enter data into the cell using the keyboard; the data may be text, numeric or formula, and appears in the cell and in the formula bar. Fill the required cells in the same way, then save the workbook (Ctrl+S).

Q: Lab Activity 2 (iii): Modify columns, rows and cells.

Ans: Modify data by clicking a cell and typing/editing its contents in the cell or formula bar. Column widths and row heights can be adjusted using the ruler or the Ribbon (in Excel, select the column/row and set the width/height), cells can be selected as a range, and their formatting changed from the Home tab groups (Font, Alignment, Number, Styles). Renaming a sheet is done by right-clicking its tab and choosing Rename.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (iv): Insert new column and row in it.

Ans: Following the book's table method: place the cursor in the row/column next to where the new one is required, right-click to open the pop-up menu, select Insert, then select Insert Rows Above or Insert Rows Below for a row, or Insert Columns to the Left or Insert Columns to the Right for a column. In the worksheet the same Insert commands in the Cells group on the Home tab insert a new row above / column to the left of the selected cell.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (v): Copy some contents from range of cells and paste it in new location.

Ans: Select the range of cells to copy and press Ctrl+C (Copy) — the contents are placed on the clipboard and remain at the source. Select the new cell where the contents are to be pasted and press Ctrl+V (Paste); the copied contents appear at the new location, as with Copy-Paste in Word.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (vi): Add new formula in a cell and copy it to 5 more cells under it by dragging the fill handle down.

Ans: Click the cell where the formula will be defined, type the equal sign (=) to let Excel know a formula is being defined, type the formula (e.g. using cell addresses such as =B2+B3) and press Enter. Then position the cursor over the fill handle of that cell until the white cross becomes a thin black cross, drag it down over the 5 cells below until they are highlighted, and release the mouse button — the formula is copied (Autofilled) into all 5 cells, with relative references adjusting automatically.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (vii): Using Paste Special command only paste formats of a cell into another cell.

Ans: Copy the contents of the cell whose formats are to be pasted. Select the new cell where Paste Special is required. Right-click and select the Paste Special command; in the Paste Special dialog box choose the Formats option — which pastes only the cell formatting of the copied data — and click OK. Only the formats are pasted into the other cell, not its values or formulas.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (viii): Create a Simple Formula that Adds Two Numbers.

Ans: Click the cell where the formula will be defined (B4, for example). Type the equal sign (=) to let Excel know a formula is being defined. Type the first number to be added (e.g. 60). Type the addition sign (+) to let Excel know an add operation is to be performed. Type the second number to be added (e.g. 70), giving =60+70. Press Enter or click the Enter button on the Formula bar to complete the formula; the result appears in the cell.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (ix): Create an absolute reference in your sheet.

Ans: Select the cell where you wish to write the formula (E2 in the book's example). Type (=) to let Excel know a formula is being defined. Click on the first cell to be included in the formula (C2, for example) and on the second cell (D2, for example). Add a $ sign before the D and a $ sign before the 2, making $D$2, to create an absolute reference; the $ sign makes the reference absolute, so cell D2 remains constant in the formula even when it is copied to another location (e.g. in E3 the formula reads =SUM(C3,$D$2)).

Q: Lab Activity 2 (x): Use different functions in your sheet.

Ans: Functions are predefined formulas beginning with = followed by the function name and argument, e.g. =SUM(A3:A9). Use the common statistical functions in the sheet: SUM adds a range of cells together; AVERAGE calculates the average of a range of cells; COUNT counts the number of chosen data in a range; MAX identifies the largest number in a range; MIN identifies the smallest number in a range. Additional functions can be inserted through the Insert Function dialog box (More Functions), selecting the function and clicking OK.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (xi): Calculate the Sum of a Range of Data Using AutoSum.

Ans: Select the Formulas tab and locate the Function Library group, from where all available functions can be accessed. Select the cell where the function is to appear (B9 in the book's example). Select the drop-down arrow next to the AutoSum command and select SUM; a formula such as =SUM(B2:B8) appears in the selected cell, AutoSum automatically selecting the range of cells based on where the function was inserted (the range can be altered if necessary). Press the Enter key or the Enter button on the formula bar and the total appears.

Q: Lab Activity 2 (xii): Create a chart of your sheet data.

Ans: Select the worksheet to work with and enter the data in all the required rows and columns, ensuring no row or column remains blank. Select the cells you want to create the chart from, including the column titles and the row labels. Click the Insert tab and hover over each Chart option in the Charts group to learn about it. Select one of the Chart options (in the book's example, Columns) and select a type of chart from the list that appears (e.g. 3-D Clustered Column); the chart appears in the worksheet with the source data.

Q: Lab Activity 3: Create a new Urdu document in InPage and write an essay on the topic "Hamara Pakistan" and Save your document.

Ans: Install and run the InPage Urdu editor (its data handling is the same as MS Word). In the File menu click the New command; the New Document dialog box appears — select the necessary options (page size, margins, direction Right To Left) and press OK, and the working window appears. Type the essay on 'Hamara Pakistan' in Urdu using InPage's fonts and tools, format it as required, and save the document when finished (File > Save).
