lessons.title: Differentiate the Following
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An analog signal is continuous; a digital signal uses 1 for ON and 0 for OFF.
  • Guided media use a physical path; unguided media broadcast through air.
  • Data rate counts bits per second; baud rate counts signal changes per second.
  • A router joins different networks; a switch connects computers on one network.
  • Radio waves travel long distances; microwaves need line-of-sight stations.
  • Synchronous transmission has no start/stop bits; asynchronous uses start and stop bits.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Differentiate the Following

Q: Q.3 (i) Analog signal vs. digital signal.

Ans: An analog signal is a continuous electrical wave with variations between the waves; in a continuous wave there are high and low values and a variety of values exist between them, as shown in Figure 4.2(a). Light waves, sound waves and radio waves are examples of analog signals, and voice data is transferred over the phone line in this form. A digital signal is discontinuous and transmits binary data based on two digits: 1 means ON and 0 means OFF. It is like a square or clock wave that perceives information as a string of impulses, where a low pulse or no pulse indicates 0 and a high pulse detects 1, and the computer accepts and processes data in this form.

Q: Q.3 (ii) Guided vs. Unguided transmission media.

Ans: Guided media use a physical path to transmit the signals, whereas unguided media broadcast the signal through the air. Guided media are also called wired communication or bounded transmission media, whereas unguided media are also called wireless communication or unbounded transmission media. Guided media provide direction to the signal, while unguided media do not direct the signal. Twisted pair cable, coaxial cable and fiber optic cable are guided media, while radio waves, microwaves, infrared and satellite are unguided media.

Q: Q.3 (iii) Data rate vs. baud rate

Ans: Data rate or bit rate is the speed at which binary digits (bits) are transmitted over a communication path, expressed in bits per second (bps); it is the measure of the number of data bits (0s and 1s) transmitted in one second in a communication channel, e.g. 2400 bits per second means 2400 zeros or ones can be transmitted in one second. Baud rate is the number of times a signal changes its state per second, e.g. a 1000 baud rate means the signal can change state a thousand times per second, and it is associated with modems, digital televisions and telephones. The two are connected by the formulae: Data rate (bps) = Baud rate (baud per second) x the number of bits per baud, and Baud rate = Data rate (bps) / the number of bits per baud.

Q: Q.3 (iv) Router vs. switch

Ans: A router is a hardware device which routes data to destination computers and connects two different logical and physical networks together: it receives data, analyzes it and then forwards it to another network, deciding the best route and distance between the two networks, and it is commonly used at home and in organizations to share a single Internet connection to multiple networks. A switch is used in a networking environment to connect computers to the same network, using each computer's unique MAC (Media Access Control) address for communication. The switch only filters and forwards network packets, so it is more intelligent than a hub but not than a router, which joins different networks instead of devices on one network.

Q: Q.3 (v) Radio wave vs. microwave

Ans: Radio waves are a wireless transmission medium used to communicate information through radio signals in air over long distances such as between cities and countries; this broadcast radio medium needs a transmitter to send signals and a receiver with an antenna in the range of the signal, its data transmission speed is up to 54 Mbps, and it is used in standard broadcast radio and television, shortwave radio, navigation and air-traffic control. Microwaves are radio waves that provide a high speed transmission from one station to another, where each microwave station contains an antenna, a transceiver and other equipment. Microwave transmission is line-of-sight transmission, so the signals travel in a straight path and cannot bend, the stations are placed on high towers or buildings within 20 to 30 miles of each other with no hurdles between them, and each station receives signals from the previous station.

Q: Q.3 (vi) Synchronous vs. asynchronous transmission modes

Ans: In synchronous transmission, data is transmitted block-by-block or word-by-word simultaneously, and large blocks of bytes are transmitted at regular intervals without any start/stop signals, with no gap between the characters. It requires a special synchronized clock to schedule the transmission and both the sending and receiving devices must be synchronized before data is transmitted; it requires more expensive equipment but provides greater speed and accuracy, and is best for communication between printers and computer. Asynchronous transmission is also called start/stop transmission because communication can start at any time and stop at any time: a start bit 0 marks the beginning of a byte, a stop bit 1 marks its end, and a parity bit is sometimes included for error checking. It does not occur at predetermined or regular intervals, data is transmitted intermittently instead of in a steady stream with gaps between data units, the timing of the signal is unimportant, and it is relatively slower and inefficient than synchronous transmission.

mcqs.q: How is an analog signal best described?
options: A continuous wave with many values between high and low
A signal with only two values
A signal that is always OFF
mcqs.why: An analog signal is a continuous electrical wave with high and low values and a variety of values between them, like sound and light waves.

mcqs.q: In a digital signal, what do 1 and 0 represent?
mcqs.why: A digital signal transmits binary data where 1 means ON and 0 means OFF, as a high pulse for 1 and a low or no pulse for 0.

mcqs.q: What is the defining feature of guided media?
options: They need no cable or path
They use a physical path to transmit signals
mcqs.why: Guided media use a physical path and are called wired or bounded media, including twisted pair, coaxial and fiber optic cables.

mcqs.q: Unguided media are also known by which name?
mcqs.why: Unguided media broadcast the signal through air without direction and are called wireless communication or unbounded transmission media.

mcqs.q: Data rate is measured as what?
options: Number of data bits transmitted in one second
mcqs.why: Data rate or bit rate is the number of data bits transmitted in one second in a channel, expressed in bits per second.

mcqs.q: How is baud rate related to data rate?
options: Data rate equals baud rate multiplied by bits per baud
Baud rate is always in bps only
Data rate equals baud rate divided by distance
mcqs.why: The solved formulae state Data rate in bps equals Baud rate multiplied by the number of bits per baud.

mcqs.q: What does a router connect together?
options: Computers on the same network only
Two different logical and physical networks
mcqs.why: A router receives data, analyses it and forwards it to another network, connecting two different logical and physical networks.

mcqs.q: What address does a switch use for communication?
mcqs.why: A switch connects computers to the same network using each computer unique MAC, Media Access Control, address for communication.

mcqs.q: Why must microwave stations be placed on high towers?
options: Microwave transmission is line-of-sight and travels in a straight path
mcqs.why: Microwaves travel in a straight path and cannot bend, so stations sit on high towers 20 to 30 miles apart with no hurdles between them.

mcqs.q: How does asynchronous transmission mark each byte?
options: With a start bit 0 and a stop bit 1
mcqs.why: Asynchronous or start/stop transmission marks the beginning of a byte with a start bit 0 and its end with a stop bit 1, unlike synchronous blocks.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A communication system has sender, receiver, message, protocol and transmission medium.
  • Communication devices convert digital signals to analog and back for telephone lines.
  • Twisted pair, coaxial and fiber optic are the guided media types.
  • Fiber optic cable transmits as light at up to gigabits per second.
  • Attenuation, distortion, noise and crosstalk are transmission impairments.
  • A dialup modem speed is measured in bps and kbps, with 56k the fastest dialup speed.
  • A NIC uses an Ethernet cable with an RJ45 connector in a LAN.
  • Fiber optic is the best medium due to high speed and no EMI.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Descriptive Questions

Q: Q.4 What is data communication? Explain the basic components of a communication system.

Ans: Data Communication (DC) is the process of using computing and communication technologies to transfer data from one place to another, or between participating parties, via some form of transmission medium such as wire cable, wireless system, microwave system or satellite system; the communicating devices must be part of a communication system, which may consist of hardware and software, and data is transmitted electronically from one system to another using standard methods, e.g. a personal computer connecting to the Internet with a modem. Figure 4.3, Components of a Communication System, shows all five basic components together: the SENDER (a computer) on the left and the RECEIVER (a computer) on the right, each with a PROTOCOL (Rules) box above it, the MESSAGE travelling from the sender side to the receiver side along the upper path, and the TRANSMISSION MEDIA as the connecting path between the two computers below. (1) Sender: a device used in a communication system to send or transmit data to another device, also called Transmitter or Source; it may send some kind of idea, perception, feeling or datum, and may be a computer, workstation, telephone handset, video camera, mobile phone, radio or TV station. (2) Receiver: a device used in a communication system to receive messages from another device (sender), also called destination; it may be a computer, workstation, telephone handset, television set, printer, fax machine or radio set. (3) Message: the piece of information or data that is to be transferred from source to intended destination; it may consist of text, numbers, pictures, sounds, videos or any combination of these, shown in Figure 4.1 as the sender's words 'Hi, how are you?'. (4) Protocol: a set of rules that guides (or governs) data communication and represents an agreement between the communicating devices; without a proper protocol the devices may be connected but cannot communicate with each other, and it may include error detection, synchronization, signaling and authentication. (5) Transmission Medium: the path or channel through which the message is transmitted (sent) or received from one location to another, e.g. twisted pair cable, fiber optic cable, microwave or satellite system, and the sender must choose a proper medium otherwise the message might not be conveyed to the desired recipients. The book also notes that feedback is an important component: once the receiver receives the message, feedback is given to the sender, which helps the sender analyze and confirm the correct interpretation of the message by the receiver.

Q: Q.5 Why communication devices are used in a communication system? Explain with reason.

Ans: A communication device is a hardware device that can send and receive data on the network, and communication devices are used on both ends of the connections in a communication system. They are needed because the signals travelling on a communication line are not always in the form the computer uses: most communication devices have the ability to convert the digital signal into analog signal over the telephone line so that the signals can be transmitted on the communication line to another end, and the reverse is also true at the receiving end. For example, data is communicated through telephone lines in the form of analog signals, so digital data from one computer must be converted into analog before transmitting and analog data received must be converted back to digital before saving it into the computer, which is the work of the modem. Devices such as the dialup modem, Network Interface Card, router and switch/access point are therefore used to establish the link between devices, route data to its destination and connect computers so that data communication can actually take place.

Q: Q.6 What is guided transmission media? Explain different types of guided media with advantages and disadvantages of each.

Ans: In guided transmission media, communication devices are directly linked with each other via physical materials (like cables, etc.) for data communication; it restricts and guides the transmission signal, is also called physical or wired transmission media, and is usually used in LAN (Local Area Network). (1) Twisted pair cable: one of the most commonly used media in LANs for connecting computers and other devices, made of two separate copper wires covered by insulating material such as plastic and twisted together to form a cable, where one wire carries signals to the receiver and the other is used only as ground reference, and the twist provides protection from Electromagnetic Interference (EMI); it is of two types, Shielded Twisted Pair (STP), which has a foil shielding layer that reduces EMI, and Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP), which has no foil shield. Its advantages are that it is less costly and its installation is easy, and telephone cable wiring uses it. (2) Coaxial cable: also referred to as Coax, it carries signals of higher frequency ranges than twisted-pair cable and consists of a single solid copper wire, the inner conductor, covered by copper mesh which protects the signals from EMI, with the inner conductor surrounded by an insulating material, an outer conductor of solid metal foil (shield) and another insulating material, the whole cable protected by an external plastic cover; it is used for voice and data transmission with very high frequency such as cable TV and telephone networks and has high bandwidth and greater transmission capacity from 10 Mbps to 200 Mbps. Its advantages are that it is faster in speed than twisted pair cable and its installation is easy, while its disadvantage is that it is more costly than twisted pair cable. (3) Fiber optic cable: made of narrow strands of glass fiber called core wrapped in protective layers, the strands being thin as a human hair, with the core surrounded by a concentric layer of glass called cladding and a plastic coating called jacket covering the cladding; it transmits signals in the form of light, so its data transmission speed is very high, up to Giga bits per second. Its advantages are that it transmits data at a higher speed than other cables, it is not suffered from EMI and it is smaller in size, while its disadvantages are that it is more costly and its installation is difficult.

Q: Q.7 (i) Explain the unguided transmission media: Radio waves.

Ans: Radio waves are an unguided (wireless) transmission medium used to communicate information through radio signals in air over long distances such as between cities and countries, and are also known as the broadcast radio transmission medium. In this medium, a transmitter is required to send messages (signals) and a receiver is required to receive them, and to receive the broadcast radio signal the receiver has an antenna located in the range of the signal; some networks use a special device called a transceiver to send and receive messages in the form of radio signals, as shown in Figure 4.8 with a transmitter antenna and a receiver antenna. The data transmission speed of broadcast radio is up to 54 Mbps (Megabits per second). Radio waves are used in standard broadcast radio and television, shortwave radio, navigation and air-traffic control and even remote-controlled toys; Bluetooth is one example, covering short distance wireless technology at a rate of 1 Mbps, and built-in Bluetooth devices include PCs, cellular phones, MP3 players, printers, fax machines, microwave ovens, some remote controls and radar.

Q: Q.7 (ii) Explain the unguided transmission media: Microwaves.

Ans: Microwaves are radio waves that provide a high speed transmission, in which data, and voice, are transmitted from one station to another through microwave signals. A microwave station contains an antenna, a transceiver (transmitter and receiver) and other equipment required for microwave communication. Microwave uses line-of-sight transmission, which means that in a microwave transmission system the data signals travel in a straight path and cannot bend. Microwave stations or antennas are usually installed on high towers or buildings and need to be placed within 20 to 30 miles of each other, each station receiving signals from the previous station, and there must be no hurdles between the transmissions of these signals, as illustrated in Figure 4.9.

Q: Q.7 (iii) Explain the unguided transmission media: Satellite.

Ans: A communication satellite is a space station that receives microwave signals from an earth microwave station (earth based station); transmitting a signal from a ground or earth station to a satellite station in space is called up-linking and the reverse is called down-linking. The first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union in 1957, and nowadays television and radio broadcast, Global Positioning Systems (GPS) and the Internet also use communication satellites. The communication satellite is launched about 22300 miles (or more) above the earth into space and consists of a solar powered transceiver that receives and sends signals. The signals are transmitted from one earth station to the satellite, the satellite receives and amplifies the signals and sends them to another earth station, as depicted in Figure 4.11; this entire process takes only a few seconds, more than one satellite is required to communicate information from one country to another country, and the data transmission speed of a communication satellite is very high, up to 1 Gbps.

Q: Q.8 What are transmission impairments? Explain different causes of transmission impairments.

Ans: Transmission impairments are the problems in the transmission media that cause information to be lost: if the transmission media were perfect, the receiver would receive exactly the same signal that the transmitter sent, but communication media are not perfect, so the received signal is not the same as the transmitted signal — what is sent is not what is received. (1) Attenuation: it is the loss of energy as the signal propagates outwards, and the amount of energy lost depends on the frequency; if the attenuation is too much, the receiver may not be able to detect the signal at all, so for reliable communication the range of frequencies of transmission should be constant, and amplification — the act of increasing signal strength by an amplifier, with decibel measuring the relative power — is the solution to attenuation. (2) Distortion: the signal changes its shape and form, because a signal is composed of multiple frequencies and each frequency in a signal has a different propagation speed through the medium, so they do not reach the destination at the same time, producing a different shape of signal as compared to the shape at the sending end; it is mostly found in sound generated or received by a computer, video or display signals and data cables such as network cables. (3) Noise: an unwanted signal that is created during data transmission, and several types of noise such as crosstalk may corrupt the signal, as Figure 4.14 shows the received signal differing from the transmitted signal because of noise in the medium. (4) Crosstalk: the effect of one wire on the other, where one wire acts as a sending antenna and the other as a receiving antenna; transmission of data over a network is difficult in the presence of crosstalk, it can cause errors and noise or prevent cables from transmitting data, and for example when talking on the telephone the listener can hear another conversation in the background, which is cross talk.

Q: Q.9 Explain any five communication devices.

Ans: The book's section 4.3 lists the most important communication devices as the dialup modem, Network Interface Card (NIC), router and switch / access point. (1) Dialup Modem: a dial-up is a connection established using a modem, used on both ends of the connection for data communication between computers through a telephone line; the modem (Modulator-Demodulator) is an electronic device that converts digital signals into analog signals and analog signals into digital signals, its speed is measured in bps and kbps, and nowadays a 56k speed is considered the fastest speed while using a dialup modem, with types including onboard, internal, external and removable modems. (2) Network Interface Card (NIC): also referred to as a LAN adapter or simply LAN card, it is used in a Local Area Network to establish the communication link between the devices (computers, printers and other devices) attached on the network through an Ethernet cable along with an RJ45 connector, and that cable connects the computer with a router which provides broadband connection to the computer. (3) Router: a hardware device which routes data to destination computers, helping in connecting two different logical and physical networks together; it receives data, analyzes it and then forwards it to another network, decides the best route and distance between the two networks, some routers also support wireless connections, and routers are commonly used at home and in different organizations to share a single Internet connection to multiple networks. (4) Switch: an important communication device used in a networking environment to connect computers to the same network; in the network every computer has a unique address for identification called a MAC (Media Access Control) address, the switch uses the MAC address for communication, and it is more intelligent than a hub but not than a router because it filters and forwards network packets only. (5) Access Point: named in the book together with the switch, as 'Switch / Access Point', in the list of the most important communication devices used on both ends of the connections in a communication system; the book describes this heading through the switch, which connects computers to the same network using MAC addresses.

Q: Q.10 Which is the best transmission medium? Explain with properties.

Ans: On the properties given in the book, the fiber optic cable is the best transmission medium. It is made of narrow strands of glass fiber called core that are wrapped in protective layers and transmits signals in the form of light; the strands are thin as a human hair, the core is surrounded by a concentric layer of glass called cladding, and a plastic coating called jacket covers the cladding. Because it uses light to transmit data, its data transmission speed is very high, up to Giga bits per second, higher than the other cables, and telephone, Internet and television companies are replacing their existing cables with fiber-optic cables. Its other properties are that it is not suffered from EMI (Electromagnetic Interference) and it is smaller in size. Its limitations, also given in the book, are that it is more costly and its installation is difficult; the fiber cabling must not be bent more than the diameter of your hand, as bending it further could cause physical damage, the connections and connectors should always be kept clean, and the tip of the actual fiber cabling must not be touched, as it could cut your finger.

lessons.title: Differentiate the Following
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Transmission is sending data through a medium, communication is the whole exchange
  • Server performs activities on client requests, client is the workstation
  • Ring forms a closed loop, Mesh gives every device a dedicated link
  • LAN covers a limited area, WAN spans countries and costs more
  • Peer to Peer has no central server, Point to Point has only two nodes
  • Dial-up reaches only 56 Kbps, DSL modem is much faster

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Differentiate the following.

Q: Q.3 (i) Data transmission vs. data communication.

Ans: Data transmission means sending and receiving data through a transmission medium. Data communication is the exchange of data between devices (computers) via some form of transmission medium, such as wire cable, wireless system, microwave system or satellite system, or via guided or unguided media. So transmission is the sending and receiving of data through the medium, while communication is the whole exchange of data between the devices.

Q: Q.3 (ii) Client vs. Server.

Ans: A server is a powerful computer which is responsible to perform activities according to the request sent to it by clients; examples are web servers, mail servers and file servers, for example a print server sends a print command to the printer when a client requests a print. A client is any other computer, also called a workstation, connected to that dedicated server usually through a hub or switch. The client sends requests to the server and receives the service or data from it.

Q: Q.3 (iii) Ring topology vs. Mesh topology.

Ans: In Ring topology, each node is connected to two adjacent nodes in the form of a closed ring or loop, the last node connects to the first node to complete the ring, and there is no dedicated connection between the nodes; data is communicated in one direction from one node to the next until it reaches its destination, and if any single connection is damaged the whole network is affected. In Mesh topology, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device, and the link carries traffic only between the two devices it connects. Mesh is fast because the message transfers directly from source to destination, but it is an expensive network needing a large quantity of cables.

Q: Q.3 (iv) LAN vs. WAN.

Ans: A Local Area Network (LAN) connects computers and devices in a limited geographic area, such as one building, one office, or a group of buildings close together, for example university departments; resources can be easily shared on it and work can be saved on a centralized server. A Wide Area Network (WAN) is a communications network that covers a wide geographical area, such as a country or the world, and connects computers across the globe at multiple sites. The main example of WAN is the Internet, which is accessible everywhere and in which devices are connected through telephone lines. WAN is more expensive than LAN and its resource management is difficult.

Q: Q.3 (v) Peer to Peer network vs. Point to Point network.

Ans: A Peer to Peer (P2P) network has no controller or central computer or dedicated server; all computers are independent and every workstation is responsible for its own activities. It is very cost effective and its maintenance is simple, but it supports a lesser number of computers in the network and its security level is not very high. A Point-to-Point network is one of the simplest networks because it only involves two nodes, joined by a direct link between those two nodes only.

Q: Q.3 (vi) Dial-up modem vs. DSL modem.

Ans: A Dial-up modem is a communication device that sends and receives data over telephone lines to and from computers; both the sending and receiving computers must have dial-up modems, and a dial-up connection must be established each time the modem is used. Its speed is very slow, with a transfer rate up to 56 Kbps, and it has now vanished as broadband is used nowadays. A DSL modem is a broadband modem used to connect a Personal Computer (PC) to the Internet; it transmits data from a PC to a DSL line at the sender end and receives data from the DSL line to the PC at the receiver end. DSL modems are much faster than ISDN modems, are designed for use with high-speed DSL connections, and are typically external, connecting to a computer via a USB or Ethernet port.

mcqs.why: The solved comparison states that in ring topology, if any single connection is damaged the whole network is affected, whereas mesh has alternative routes for the data.

mcqs.why: A LAN connects computers in a limited geographic area such as university departments in nearby buildings, where resources are easily shared and work can be saved on a centralized server.

mcqs.why: A peer-to-peer network has no controller, central computer or dedicated server; it is cost effective and simple to maintain but supports fewer computers and has lower security.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Resource sharing lets all computers share one printer or hard disk
  • Simplex is one-way, Half-duplex is one direction at a time, Full-duplex is simultaneous
  • Network architecture has three types: Client/Server, Peer to Peer, Point to Point
  • MAN spans a city or state, between LAN and WAN in size
  • Mesh channels for n devices equal n(n-1)/2, so 6 devices need 15
  • DSL modem is the fastest modem, DSL lines reach 1 Mbps to 100 Mbps
  • Dial-up lines transfer at 2400 bps to 56 Kbps and are the cheapest

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.4 What are different uses of computer networks? Explain in detail.

Q: Q.4 What are different uses of computer networks? Explain in detail.

Ans: (a) Resource sharing: it is one of the most popular uses of computer networks; a printer shared on a network saves a lot of investment in hardware, because all connected computers can use that printer instead of having separate printers, and scanners, fax machines and hard disks can also be shared, while in software resources a data file or a licensed copy of software can be shared. (b) Communication: networks are the backbone of daily communication in offices and organizations; software transmits messages and emails at fast speed, a person can communicate with a single individual or a group, for example in online meetings, and live video conferencing is used for important discussions, online education and online medical suggestions from distant experts. (c) Data sharing: documents, files, account information, reports and multimedia can be shared with the help of computer networks, application sharing is allowed in many organizations such as banks and small firms, and email has enabled members of a company separated by geographical locations to send reports and analyse data. (d) E-Commerce: organizations do business with customers over the Internet, for example online shopping, air ticket reservation, paying utility bills, transactions and online funds transfer in online banking, and students can access the digital library to purchase online books, magazines and research articles; the World Wide Web (WWW) is a main source of E-commerce facilities on the Internet.

Exercise — Q.5 Explain different modes of data transmission with examples and diagrams.

Q: Q.5 Explain different modes of data transmission with examples and diagrams.

Ans: The term transmission mode defines the direction of data flow between two linked communicating devices in a network; there are three modes. (1) Simplex: data flows only in one direction from the sending device to the receiving device, for example TV transmission. Diagram (in words): a Sending Device on the left, a single one-way arrow pointing right labelled with the data flow, and a Receiving Device on the right; no arrow returns. (2) Half-duplex: data can flow in both directions from the sending device to the receiving device and back, but only in one direction at a time, for example a walkie-talkie. Diagram (in words): Device A on the left and Device B on the right joined by one link, with an arrow from A to B for one turn and an arrow from B to A for the next turn, the two arrows never active at the same time. (3) Full-duplex: data can flow in both directions at the same time, so both communicating parties can talk simultaneously, for example on a telephone; it allows interactive communication and enhances efficiency, though because of two simplex links the cost of the medium increases. Diagram (in words): Device A on the left and Device B on the right joined by two separate links, one arrow going from A to B on the upper link and another arrow going from B to A on the lower link at the same time.

Exercise — Q.6 What is network architecture? Explain different types of network architecture.

Q: Q.6 What is network architecture? Explain different types of network architecture.

Ans: Network architecture is the design of a communication network. It is a framework for the specification of a network's physical components and their functional organization and configuration, its operational principles and procedures, as well as the data formats used in its operation; it is the physical and logical design of the software, hardware, protocols and media of data transmission, and shows how computers are organized and how tasks are allocated to the computer. The three types are: (1) Client and Server network, in which one computer is a dedicated computer called the server (web, mail and file servers) and all other computers, called clients or workstations, are connected to it usually through a hub or switch, and the server performs activities according to the requests sent by clients. (2) Peer to Peer network, which has no controller, central computer or dedicated server; every workstation is responsible for its own activities, it is very cost effective but supports a lesser number of computers. (3) Point to Point network, one of the simplest networks because it only involves two nodes joined directly.

Exercise — Q.7 Explain different types of networks on the basis of spatial distance.

Q: Q.7 Explain different types of networks on the basis of spatial distance.

Ans: (1) Local Area Network (LAN): it connects computers and devices in a limited geographic area, such as one building, one office, or a group of buildings close together, for example university departments; software and hardware resources can be easily shared on it, work can be saved on a centralized server, and a single Internet connection can be shared among connected users. (2) Metropolitan Area Network (MAN): it is a communication network spanning a city or a state, a mid-range network smaller than WAN but larger than LAN; it may be a single network such as a cable television network, or a means of connecting a number of LANs to interlink branches of offices in a city so that resources may be shared, and many cellular phone systems are MANs. (3) Wide Area Network (WAN): it is a communication network that spans a wide geographical area across the globe, linking a variety of computers from mainframes to terminals at multiple sites, for example the ATMs of banks and NADRA branches connecting through WAN; the main example of WAN is the Internet, which is accessible everywhere and in which devices are connected through telephone lines.

Exercise — Q.8 What is network topology? Explain Mesh topology along with advantages and disadvantages and also draw its diagram.

Q: Q.8 What is network topology? Explain Mesh topology along with advantages and disadvantages and also draw its diagram.

Ans: Network topology is the physical layout of joining a number of computers in the form of a network, that is, the way of physically connecting computers or nodes on a network; its main types are Bus, Ring, Star and Mesh. In Mesh topology, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device, and the dedicated link carries traffic only between the two devices it connects; it is fast because the message transfers directly from source to destination, a fully connected mesh has n(n-1)/2 physical channels to link n devices and every device must have n-1 input/output ports, and it is used in WAN instead of LAN, usually as a backbone of a hybrid network. Advantages: multiple links are used, so if a route breaks down the other routes transfer the data; it manages heavy traffic because each device transmits data simultaneously; if one device breaks down the rest of the network works smoothly; and adding and removal of devices are very easy. Disadvantages: it is an expensive network; a large quantity of cables are required; and installation and configuration is difficult and time consuming. Diagram (in words): six nodes, each labelled Computer, are placed around a shape — one at the top, one at the upper left, one at the upper right, one at the lower left, one at the lower right and one at the bottom (Figure 5.17) — and every Computer is joined by a straight dedicated line to every other Computer, so the lines cross each other in the middle forming a complete web with no central hub, switch or server.

Exercise — Q.9 Explain different types of Modems. Which one is the fastest modem in term of speed?

Q: Q.9 Explain different types of Modems. Which one is the fastest modem in term of speed?

Ans: The types of modem are Dial-up modem, DSL modem and ISDN modem. A Dial-up modem is a communication device that sends and receives data over telephone lines to and from computers; both the sending and receiving computers must have dial-up modems, a connection must be established each time it is used, and its speed is very slow compared to broadband, with a transfer rate up to 56 Kbps. A DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) modem is a broadband modem used to connect a Personal Computer (PC) to the Internet; it transmits data from a PC to a DSL line at the sender end and receives data from the DSL line to the PC at the receiver end, and it is typically external and connects via a USB or Ethernet port. An ISDN modem is used for an ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) connection that can transmit digital data, voice and video from a PC to an ISDN line and also receives digital data from the ISDN line; it transmits information much faster than a typical dial-up modem and its data transfer rate is up to 1.54 Mbps. The DSL modem is the fastest of these, because DSL modems are much faster than ISDN modems, which are in turn faster than dial-up modems.

Exercise — Q.10 Compare different data communication lines in terms of data transfer rate and cost.

Q: Q.10 Compare different data communication lines in terms of data transfer rate and cost.

Ans: Dial-up Lines: transfer rate 2400 bps to 56 Kbps, and they are the cheapest; they are inexpensive and available everywhere, but they are slow and low quality, and speed may degrade due to the amount of line noise. ISDN: transfer rate 64 Kbps to 1.54 Mbps, and it is costly than dial-up lines; it is faster than dial-up and uses conventional phone lines, but it is more expensive than dial-up lines. DSL: transfer rate 1 Mbps to 100 Mbps, and it is cheaper than ISDN but costly than dial-up; it gives fast download, is always on and has higher security, but it needs to be closer to the phone company. So in speed DSL is the fastest, then ISDN, then dial-up, while in cost dial-up is the cheapest, then DSL, then ISDN.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Computer security is also known as information security
  • A computer crime offender can attack from a distance through the network
  • Cracking modifies software to bypass registration and payment options
  • A worm spreads independently, a virus depends on a host file
  • Authentication verifies identity, authorization verifies access level
  • Biometrics uses face, fingerprints, irises, voice or typing rhythm
  • Multimodal access needs more than one method, like thumb plus face

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.3 Give short answers to the following questions.

Q: Q.3 (i) What is computer security?

Ans: Computer security is a branch of computer technology known as information security as applied to computers and networks. Its objective is the protection of the computer system and its resources from unauthorized access, corruption or natural disaster. It allows the information and property to remain accessible and productive to its authentic and authorized users only.

Q: Q.3 (ii) What is the difference between a computer crime and a conventional crime?

Ans: A computer crime, or cybercrime, is any crime that involves a computer and a network and is performed by an expert user called a hacker. It includes accessing a computer in an unauthorized way, altering input or stored data, fraud, copyright violation and spamming, and the harm is done to data, software and information. A conventional crime does not involve a computer or a network as the means of committing it. In computer crime the offender may attack the system from a distance through the network, without physically reaching the victim.

Q: Q.3 (iii) Differentiate between hacking and cracking.

Ans: Hacking is gaining unauthorized access to computers or telecommunications systems. A hacker may steal the information of a client/server, credit card information and system passwords, and may hack an email password and use an account without the owner's knowledge; hacking done to expose security flaws for companies is called White hat hacking and illegal hacking is called Black hat hacking. Cracking is different: software cracking is the modification of software to remove or disable features considered undesirable, such as bypassing the registration and payment options on a copyrighted software product or turning a demo version into a fully functional version without paying for it. The people who do cracking are called crackers.

Q: Q.3 (iv) What is the difference between a virus and a worm?

Ans: The key difference between a virus and a worm is the way in which it reproduces and spreads. A virus is dependent upon the host file or boot sector, and the transfer of files between computers spreads it. A computer worm, on the other hand, can execute completely independently and spread on its own accord through network connections. A worm replicates itself until it has consumed all the space in memory or on hard disks, leaving no vacant space for new files, so the computer may get stuck and stop working.

Q: Q.3 (v) What is adware? How a user can get rid off and remove adware?

Ans: Adware is advertising-supported software, which gets the online ads to play automatically when you visit infected websites. It downloads itself without the user's knowledge or permission during the installation of an infected program or software, records Internet surfing activities and may provide this information to advertising companies. To get rid of adware, a user should install and keep updated antivirus and anti-spyware software, because anti-spyware protects the computer against pop-ups, slow performance and security threats caused by spyware and similar programs. Such software monitors computer activities, stops the downloading of infected files and stops the infected programs from running.

Q: Q.3 (vi) How virus spread through Internet in computers?

Ans: Files shared on a network and downloaded directly from the Internet are among the fastest-growing sources of computer virus infections. If there is an infected computer in the network, exchanging files with such a system may infect your computer. There is also a possibility that if you visit infected websites and download any file from such websites, the virus may transfer into your computer and may harm your files. Viruses also spread through attached files from unknown emails downloaded from the Internet.

Q: Q.3 (vii) Differentiate between authentication and authorization.

Ans: Authentication is a process to verify the identity of a user to the computer; the system validates the user identity and then access is granted, for example through password based authentication, device based authentication, authentication apps or biometric authentication. Authorization is finding out if the person, once identified, is permitted to have the resource; it is the process that verifies the access level of resources being granted. In other words, authorization decides which resource, such as a hardware device or a data file, the user wants to access and which kind of access — read, write and delete — he or she is allowed.

Q: Q.3 (viii) Compare authorized access with unauthorized access.

Ans: Authorized access is the use of a computer, data, or network with permission. Unauthorized access is the use of computers, data or network without permission. System administrators view any kind of unauthorized access as a threat and usually try to pursue offenders vigorously. Hackers who gain unauthorized access are heavily fined as well as given imprisonment in a court of law.

Q: Q.3 (ix) What is biometric technology? Give one example.

Ans: Biometrics is a form of authentication that provides authentication based on the biological features of a person, using physical characteristics like a human face, fingerprints and irises, or behavioral characteristics like a human voice, handwriting or typing rhythm. Unlike keys and passwords, personal traits are extremely difficult to lose or forget and are very difficult to copy, so they are considered safer and more secure. Example: fingerprint recognition, where most laptops today come with fingerprint biometric readers, and fingerprint and palm recognition are used for authentication, as is signature recognition mostly used by banks for account holder authentication.

Q: Q.3 (x) What is multimodal authentication?

Ans: Multimodal or Multifactor authentication is the act of using more than one authentication method when logging on to a server or a workstation for accessing the resources. This form of authentication helps to provide additional security to applications or computers compared to a simple authentication mechanism. For example, a system using a single factor may grant access by thumb recognition or face recognition alone, but in multimodal authentication the system will grant the resource only if a person successfully logs in by using both thumb as well as face recognition.

options: A virus spreads on its own through networks, while a worm needs a host file
A worm is harmless, while a virus always formats the hard disk
A virus replicates in memory, while a worm never replicates at all
A worm can execute completely independently and spreads on its own through network connections, while a virus depends on a host file or boot sector
mcqs.why: A virus depends on the host file or boot sector and spreads when files are transferred, while a worm executes independently, spreads through network connections and replicates until memory or disk space is consumed.

mcqs.q: How can a user get rid of adware?
options: Install and keep updated antivirus and anti-spyware software
Share files with more computers on the network
Download more free programs from infected websites
Disable all security software on the computer
mcqs.why: To remove adware the user should install and keep updated antivirus and anti-spyware software, which monitors activities, stops infected downloads and stops infected programs from running.

mcqs.q: Which are among the fastest-growing sources of computer virus infection?
options: Files printed on a paper printer
Files shared on a network and files downloaded directly from the Internet
Files stored on a switched-off computer
Files typed by hand on a standalone computer
mcqs.why: Files shared on a network and downloaded directly from the Internet are among the fastest-growing sources of virus infection, along with attachments in emails from unknown senders.

mcqs.q: Once a user's identity has been verified, authorization is the process that:
options: Checks the user's fingerprint against a stored scan
Creates a new password for the user account
Verifies the access level of resources being granted, such as read, write and delete access
Deletes the user's account from the system
mcqs.why: Authentication verifies who the user is, while authorization finds out whether the identified person is permitted the resource and which kind of access, read, write or delete, is allowed.

mcqs.q: How do system administrators and the law treat unauthorized access?
options: It is allowed whenever the hacker finds a security flaw
It carries no penalty because no physical property is touched
It is treated the same as authorized access with permission
It is viewed as a threat, and hackers who gain it are heavily fined and given imprisonment
mcqs.why: Authorized access is use with permission and unauthorized access is use without permission; administrators treat it as a threat and offenders are heavily fined and imprisoned by a court of law.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of biometric authentication given in the book?
options: Fingerprint recognition, as in the fingerprint readers built into most laptops today
Typing a secret numeric PIN at an ATM machine
Showing a magnetic-strip card to a card reader
Entering a username and a strong password
mcqs.why: Biometrics uses physical traits like face, fingerprints and irises or behavioral traits like voice and typing rhythm; fingerprint recognition in laptops is the example given in the solved answer.

mcqs.q: In multimodal authentication, when is access to the resource granted?
options: As soon as any single method, such as thumb recognition alone, succeeds
Only if the person successfully logs in using more than one method, such as both thumb and face recognition
Immediately, without any authentication method at all
Only after the user shares the password with the administrator
mcqs.why: Multimodal authentication uses more than one method when logging on; for example access is granted only if a person succeeds with both thumb recognition and face recognition.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Security protects resources with passwords, multifactor authentication, encryption and firewalls
  • Spamming sends junk emails to thousands of unknown addresses
  • Denial of Service attacks crash the computer network
  • Resident viruses dwell in RAM, Trojans disguise as useful software
  • Michelangelo is a time bomb virus that formats data files on March 6
  • Every spyware is malware, but malware also covers viruses, worms and Trojans
  • Windows Defender is the built-in antivirus in the latest Windows

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Q.4 What is the importance of computer security?

Q: Q.4 What is the importance of computer security?

Ans: Security of computers is rapidly gaining importance in today's world where almost every day important confidential online documents and information have the possibility of being stolen online. Computer security generally deals with processes by which valuable data can be protected and preserved, in both their theoretical and practical aspects. The purpose of computer security is to secure a particular computer system from any kind of crime, so it aims at securing data, keeping them intact and also providing uninterrupted services. Its major aim is to protect hardware and software resources by applying strong passwords, multifactor authentication techniques, encryption techniques and firewalls.

Exercise — Q.5 What is cybercrime? Explain different types of cybercrime.

Q: Q.5 What is cybercrime? Explain different types of cybercrime.

Ans: Cybercrime refers to any crime that involves a computer and a network, performed by an expert user called a hacker. Its types given in the unit are: (1) Accessing a computer in an unauthorized way for spreading viruses or malware on it. (2) Altering computer input in an unauthorized way, and altering or deleting stored data. (3) Other forms of fraud facilitated using computer systems, including bank fraud, identity theft, extortion and theft of classified information. (4) Copyright violation, where someone's copyrighted products are used and distributed without prior consent. (5) Spamming, where junk emails are distributed to thousands of unknown email addresses. The most popular network hacking attacks are Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, which crash the computer network, and mail bombs, which attack mail servers.

Exercise — Q.6 “Virus is a great threat to computers”. Why? Explain different types of computer viruses.

Q: Q.6 “Virus is a great threat to computers”. Why? Explain different types of computer viruses.

Ans: A computer virus is a kind of malicious software written intentionally to enter a computer without the user's permission or knowledge, and it may disturb the normal working process of the computer. Some viruses do little, but others can replicate and cause severe harm and adversely affect the programs and performance of the system; the hard disk may also be formatted by some viruses and we face the data loss issue, so a virus should never be assumed harmless and left on a system. Types of viruses: Resident Viruses, which are permanent and dwell in the RAM memory and corrupt files and programs that are opened, closed, copied or renamed; Boot Virus, which affects the boot sector of a hard disk; Trojans or Trojan Horses, destructive programs that disguise themselves as valuable and useful software available for download on the Internet and do not replicate themselves; Jerusalem or Logic Bomb or Time Bomb virus, a piece of code intentionally inserted into software that sets off a malicious function when specified conditions are met or on specific dates; Michelangelo, a time bomb virus that formats all data files on March 6; and SirCam, which travels as an attachment with email messages and replicates itself by automatically mailing itself to dozens of people in the victim's e-mail address book.

Exercise — Q.7 Differentiate between malware and spyware.

Q: Q.7 Differentiate between malware and spyware.

Ans: Malware stands for malicious software that includes computer viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware, dishonest adware and other malicious and unwanted software or programs, so it is the general name for all such harmful software. Spyware is one specific type of malware: it is a malicious program that collects various types of personal information, such as Internet surfing habits and sites that have been visited by users. Spyware infects the computer by downloading and installing infected software without our knowledge, and it has the capability to change computer settings, resulting in slow connection speeds, different home pages, and/or loss of Internet connection or functionality of other programs. Thus every spyware is malware, but malware also covers many other threats besides spyware.

Exercise — Q.8 What are different ways of spreading virus in computers?

Q: Q.8 What are different ways of spreading virus in computers?

Ans: There are many ways that computer viruses spread, and sometimes users know they are infected and most of the time they do not know. (1) Infected flash drives/CDs: through an infected computer, viruses can easily be copied onto a CD/DVD or flash drive, and any later use of these removable mediums will most likely infect the computer they are used with; when an infected flash drive is inserted in the USB port and opened, the virus starts activation. (2) Pirated software: pirated software is an unauthorized copy of legitimate software and usually contains viruses, and once downloading starts it is installed into the system without the user's knowledge. (3) Network and Internet: files shared on a network and downloaded directly from the Internet are among the fastest-growing sources of infection, and visiting infected websites and downloading files from them can transfer the virus. (4) E-mail attachments: most viruses are delivered through attachments, often sent from people you know; when the user opens the email and the attachment, the virus executes itself and begins to infect the system and other files, and viruses commonly spread from downloading attachments in unsolicited emails.

Exercise — Q.9 How a computer virus affects a computer system? Elaborate your answer by listing various symptoms of an attack by viruses.

Q: Q.9 How a computer virus affects a computer system? Elaborate your answer by listing various symptoms of an attack by viruses.

Ans: A virus enters the system through infected USB or hard disk, email attachments or downloads, attaches itself to data files and distributes through storage devices from one system to another, disturbing the normal working of the computer, replicating itself, harming programs and performance, and in severe cases formatting the hard disk and causing data loss. Symptoms of a virus attack are: the computer runs more slowly than normal; the computer stops responding or freezes often; the computer crashes and restarts every few minutes; the computer restarts on its own and then fails to run normally; applications on the computer do not work correctly; the applications are closing automatically; disks or disk drives are inaccessible; users cannot print correctly because of unknown messages appearing on screen; users see unusual error messages; and users see unreadable menus and dialog boxes. These are common signs of virus infection, but they might also indicate hardware or software problems, so up-to-date antivirus software is needed to be certain.

Exercise — Q.10 How a computer can be protected against virus?

Q: Q.10 How a computer can be protected against virus?

Ans: To prevent damages, virus protection and removal programs have become compulsory for computer systems, and because new viruses are created constantly, updated virus protection software is preferred. Antivirus programs are capable of locating, preventing and removing malicious programs from a computer system; the antivirus executes in the background to keep the system safe, and if any virus is detected the computer shows a warning message and asks whether the infection should be quarantined, removed, ignored or moved to the vault. Anti-spyware software also protects the computer against pop-ups, slow performance and security threats caused by spyware, monitors computer activities, filters emails and stops the downloading of infected files. The latest anti-virus software must be installed and kept updated, flash drives should be scanned with it, and in the latest Microsoft Windows operating system the built-in antivirus Windows Defender is installed with Windows.

Exercise — Q.11 Explain different Authentication Methodologies in detail.

Q: Q.11 Explain different Authentication Methodologies in detail.

Ans: (a) Username and Password: a username and password are used for authentication; the username usually reflects the name of the individual and is a combination of characters, numbers and special characters, while a strong password is a secret code that must be a combination of numbers, characters and some special characters, should not be written down or shared, and must not be a mobile number, date of birth or name, because a weak password can easily be guessed. After successfully logging in, the resources are granted and this methodology also identifies the access level of a user. (b) Personal Identification Number (PIN): a PIN is a secret numeric password or secret personal numbers shared between a user and a system, also called a passcode, used to authenticate the user to the system; the user provides a non-confidential user identifier or token (the user ID) and a confidential PIN, and PINs are most often used for Automated Teller Machines (ATMs), telephone calling cards, accessing a wireless network, and for debit cards and credit cards. (c) Access Cards: access cards or security pass cards are often used to gain entry into areas and buildings with restricted access; an access card is a type of smart card having an embedded chip or magnetic strip with encoded data that a card reader can read, the card may be for general access or individually encoded with the cardholder's ID number and access level, a PIN code is mostly associated with it, and the ATM card is the most common example. (d) Biometrics: this form of authentication provides authentication based on biological features, using physical characteristics like a human face, fingerprints and irises, or behavioral characteristics like a human voice, handwriting or typing rhythm; personal traits are extremely difficult to lose, forget or copy, biometric scans are difficult to hack and are unique and vary from person to person, and a biometric system uses a sensor, an electronic device that reads and stores the information, and software that analyzes the characteristic and performs the comparisons.

Exercise — Q.12 What are computer ethics? Give a sample code of conduct suggested by the Computer Ethics Institute (CEI).

Q: Q.12 What are computer ethics? Give a sample code of conduct suggested by the Computer Ethics Institute (CEI).

Ans: Computer ethics are some basic ethical rules that determine what is right and what is wrong; they concern the legal, professional, social and moral responsibilities of computer professionals and end-users, that is, knowing the difference between ethical and unethical acts performed by users. For example, it is easy to duplicate copyrighted digital content, but computer ethics suggest it is wrong to do so without the authors' or owners' approval, and accessing someone's personal information such as a PIN code is unethical. The sample code of conduct suggested by the Computer Ethics Institute (CEI) includes: do not use a computer to harm other people; do not snoop around in other people's computer files; do not use a computer to steal information such as a PIN code of a debit or credit card; do not use a computer to bear false witness; do not copy or use proprietary software for which you have not paid; do not use other people's computer resources without authorization or proper compensation; do not plug in a virus-infected external storage device in others' computers without their proper consent; do not copy copyrighted software illegally; avoid using the account of someone else for accessing resources without permission; always think about the social consequences of the program you are writing or the system you are designing; always make proper use of computer hardware, software and data in the computer lab and avoid the breakdown of resources; and always use a computer in ways that ensure consideration and respect for your fellow humans.

Exercise — Q.13 Explain different areas of computer ethics.

Q: Q.13 Explain different areas of computer ethics.

Ans: The major areas of computer ethics are: (1) Information Accuracy, which concerns the correct handling of 'personal information' and the correctness and quality of the data or information provided; the accurate use of such information is essential for businesses, non-profit organizations, consumers and the government, and information must be shared with trusted parties only who are bound to maintain its confidentiality. (2) Copyright and Intellectual Property Rights: intellectual property refers to creations of the intellect, an idea or a product, such as inventions, literary and artistic works, symbols, names, images, logos and designs, and an unauthorized person cannot use it without prior permission from the inventor; a copyright protects the published work from use by unauthorized persons. (3) Software Piracy, which is the illegal copying, unauthorized use or distributing of copyrighted or licensed software without the consent of the developer or owner; it is morally bad to reproduce a copy and sell it for profit or produce the same or a similar version without giving proper credit to the original author, although making one backup copy of licensed software for use only when the original fails is not immoral, and downloading licensed software from the Internet without purchasing it is piracy and a security risk. (4) Information Privacy, also called data privacy, which is the relationship between collection and distribution of data, technology and the issues related to them, and is about keeping the privacy of confidential data while distributing data to a third party; its challenge is to share data while protecting personally identifiable information and not misusing or mishandling it.

Exercise — Q.14 Why antivirus software is necessary for a computer?

Q: Q.14 Why antivirus software is necessary for a computer?

Ans: Antivirus software is necessary because antivirus programs are capable of locating, preventing and removing malicious programs from a computer system, and they have proved to be a very useful means of protecting computer systems from harmful viruses and worms. The antivirus executes in the background to keep the computer system safe from viruses, and if any virus is detected, the computer shows a warning message and confirms whether the infection should be quarantined, removed, ignored or moved to the vault. If antivirus software is not installed in the presence of a virus, the virus will harm your data, delete data, modify the files and forward spam emails to you. Because new viruses are created constantly, it is essential to keep the antivirus software updated, and antivirus and anti-spyware software are a necessity today to ensure the security of the computer and personal information.

mcqs.q: What is the major aim of computer security?
options: To protect hardware and software resources using strong passwords, multifactor authentication, encryption techniques and firewalls
To make copyrighted software free for every user
To allow every user to access every computer on a network
To replace all passwords with a single shared password
mcqs.why: Computer security aims to secure data, keep them intact and provide uninterrupted services, protecting hardware and software resources through strong passwords, multifactor authentication, encryption and firewalls.

mcqs.q: Spamming, a type of cybercrime, means:
options: A computer is accessed in an unauthorized way to spread malware
Junk emails are distributed to thousands of unknown email addresses
Stored data is altered or deleted without authorization
Copyrighted products are distributed without prior consent
mcqs.why: Spamming is the cybercrime in which junk emails are distributed to thousands of unknown email addresses; other types include unauthorized access, altering data, fraud and copyright violation.

mcqs.q: Which popular network hacking attack crashes the computer network?
mcqs.why: The most popular network hacking attacks are Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, which crash the computer network, and mail bombs, which attack mail servers.

mcqs.q: Why should a computer virus never be assumed harmless and left on a system?
options: Because every virus immediately destroys the computer monitor
Because a virus always stays completely inactive forever
Because viruses only change the desktop wallpaper of the computer
Some viruses can format the hard disk, causing data loss, and others replicate and severely harm programs and performance
mcqs.why: Some viruses do little, but others replicate, severely harm programs and performance, and some can even format the hard disk so the user faces data loss; a virus must never be left on a system.

mcqs.q: Resident viruses are harmful because they:
options: Dwell permanently in the RAM memory and corrupt files and programs that are opened, closed, copied or renamed
Affect only the boot sector of a hard disk
Disguise themselves as useful software for download and never replicate
Activate only on one fixed date in the year
mcqs.why: Resident viruses are permanent viruses that dwell in RAM memory and corrupt files and programs whenever they are opened, closed, copied or renamed.

mcqs.q: Trojan Horses are destructive programs that:
options: Dwell permanently in RAM and corrupt every opened file
Disguise themselves as valuable and useful software available for download on the Internet, and do not replicate themselves
Always travel as attachments in email messages only
Format all data files on March 6 every year
mcqs.why: Trojans disguise themselves as valuable, useful software offered for download on the Internet and, unlike viruses and worms, they do not replicate themselves.

mcqs.q: Michelangelo is a time bomb virus that:
options: Formats all data files on January 1
Mails itself to dozens of people in the address book
Formats all data files on March 6
Corrupts files stored only on flash drives
mcqs.why: Michelangelo is a time bomb virus that formats all data files on March 6, while SirCam instead travels as an email attachment and mails itself to people in the victim's address book.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly differentiates malware and spyware?
options: Spyware is the general name for all harmful software, and malware is one type of spyware
Malware and spyware are two names for exactly the same program
Spyware protects the computer, while malware collects personal information
Malware is the general name for all harmful software, and spyware is one specific type of malware that collects personal information
mcqs.why: Malware is the general name for viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware, dishonest adware and other unwanted programs; spyware is the specific malware that collects personal information such as surfing habits.

mcqs.q: When an infected flash drive is inserted into the USB port and opened, what happens?
options: The virus on it starts activation and can infect the computer
The antivirus automatically formats the flash drive
Nothing, because viruses cannot spread through removable media
The computer converts the virus into a harmless text file
mcqs.why: Viruses copy easily onto CDs, DVDs and flash drives through an infected computer, and when an infected flash drive is inserted in the USB port and opened, the virus starts activation.

mcqs.q: Which is a symptom of a virus attack on a computer?
options: The computer runs faster than normal in every program
The computer restarts on its own and then fails to run normally
All applications start working more correctly than before
Printouts always come out perfectly with no messages
mcqs.why: Symptoms of a virus attack include the computer running slowly, freezing, crashing and restarting every few minutes, restarting on its own and failing to run normally, and disks becoming inaccessible.

mcqs.q: The built-in antivirus installed with the latest Microsoft Windows operating system is:
mcqs.why: The latest antivirus must be installed and kept updated, flash drives should be scanned with it, and in the latest Microsoft Windows the built-in antivirus Windows Defender is installed with Windows; without antivirus a virus can harm or delete data, modify files and forward spam.

mcqs.q: A strong password must NOT be:
options: A combination of numbers, characters and some special characters
A secret code kept private and never shared with others
Different from the passwords used for other accounts
A mobile number, date of birth or name, because a weak password can easily be guessed
mcqs.why: A strong password combines numbers, characters and special characters and is never written down or shared; it must not be a mobile number, date of birth or name, which can easily be guessed.

mcqs.q: An access card used for entry into restricted areas is:
options: A type of smart card having an embedded chip or magnetic strip with encoded data that a card reader can read
A secret numeric password typed on a telephone keypad
A scan of the cardholder's fingerprint and iris
A paper card with the user's photograph printed on it
mcqs.why: Access cards are smart cards with an embedded chip or magnetic strip holding encoded data such as the cardholder's ID number and access level; the ATM card is the most common example.

mcqs.q: Which action does the Computer Ethics Institute (CEI) code of conduct forbid?
options: Thinking about the social consequences of a program you write
Copying or using proprietary software for which you have not paid
Using a computer with consideration and respect for fellow humans
Keeping proper care of hardware and data in the computer lab
mcqs.why: The CEI code includes: do not use a computer to harm or steal, do not snoop in others' files, and do not copy or use proprietary software for which you have not paid.

mcqs.q: Under software piracy rules, which action is NOT immoral?
options: Copying licensed software and selling the copy for profit
Downloading licensed software from the Internet without purchasing it
Making one backup copy of licensed software for use only when the original fails
Producing a similar version without giving credit to the original author
mcqs.why: Software piracy is the illegal copying or distribution of licensed software, but making one backup copy of licensed software for use only when the original fails is not immoral.
